### Reviewer 1

I enjoyed reading this manuscript by the Yazdan-Shahmorad group at UofWashington. The research details new
technological developments on a cranial window that this group has been optimizing for several years. The cranial window
allows a combination of techniques that together provide a powerful means of investigation of the primate brain. The platform
allows for both optical imaging, electrophysiology, and optogenetic stimulation simultaneously. The authors demonstrate the
ability to conduct optogenetic stimulation using an array of LED lights that can be controlled individually. They also
demonstrate the ability of this LED stimulation in combination with opsin expression to alter motor behaviour in macaque
monkeys. I specifically note the efforts of the authors to make their hardware and software publicly available for the larger
community of researchers.
I believe one of the main strength of this technique is the ability to observe the cortex, including its fluorescence, over the
course of experiments. This allows confirming that the viral vector expression is successful and still active during
experiments. The authors did notice a change in opsin expression over time, which emphasizes the importance of this
monitoring. The main limitations of the paper are, in my opinion, linked to the electrophysiological and behavioural proof of
concepts, which are not perfect. However, I believe these limitations are more a function of the opsin (Jaws) they chose for
those proofs of concept rather than the hardware they are presenting as the main purpose of this manuscript. I have only a
minor concerns below.
page 3, 3rd paragraph: Merging of optogenetic and electrical (recording) platforms ...
p.4, 3rd para: disrupting a center-ou(t) reach task
p5. 2nd para: "The MMAD, as well as the commercially available electrode array (Ripple Neuro, Salt Lake City, UT)". I could
not find the MMAD on the Ripple Neuro website. Can you please add details on how to obtain this product in the Methods?
p7, Fig.2A: Consider rotating middle left subpanel 90° to be consistent with top view
p7, "Optical Stability": The optical stability section is an important section that, unfortunately, lack supporting images and
figures. I would appreciate to see pictures of the experiments described in this paragraph to let the readers understand the
issue of tissue growth better, including it’s speed. Could some metric of “opacity” could be derived quantitatively from the
pictures? It would be nice to show this metric over time following implantations/explantations of MMAD.
p8, 2nd para: "optogenetic viral vector (AAV8-hSyn-Jaws-(*GFP*))" .
I understand more details are in the STAR methods, but it would be nice to include the total volume injected at each site, and
the viral solution titter in the main text.
p8, 3rd para: "eliminating the need for live-MRI," . To be fair, the use of MRI is not just to monitor reflux, but also to confirm
volume of diffusion live and targeting accuracy. Please nuance this statement.
I did not see a reference to Fig. 3A in the text.
p8, 4th para: "two years after infusion we observed a significant reduction of expression in both monkeys (data not shown)."
This is a very important information only available to authors using this technology. I strongly encourage adding some data
on this in the Supplement.
p10, 2nd para: "We observed increased ECoG power with the control wavelength (Fig. 4D, M), but to a significantly lesser
extent than our standard wavelength " : I am not convinced by that test, since I do not know what was the response expected
to blue light for this specific opsin. Should it be zero? If so, this would suggest that the effects observed are heat-driven, or
other artefacts.
"This suggests ECoG responses are primarily optogenetically-evoked, and not thermally-evoked" : Does blue light really
generate the same amount of heat artefacts? A more thorough test would be to stimulate over a non-transduced area to see
if heat is a culprit. (I can see the authors did that in the next figure)
Also, what to make of the different effect of light stimulation as a function of frequencies between the blue and red light?
(especially in lower frequencies)
p10, 5th para: "For both monkeys, ECoG power evoked by red LEDs was stronger in the expressing areas than the opsin
deficient areas" Shoudn’t we expect to see “no” response in opsin free areas? What might be causing this residual
response?
"where there was no significance between the opsin expressing and opsin deficient areas " This was not clear from reading
the previous section. I saw no mention to this comparison. I think this should be represented clearly, as it comes as a
surprise reading this sentence here.
Fig 4. Resolution of this figure is insufficient given size of font. This may be an error in format conversion.
Please better represent on this figure the light stimulation period and frequency over time with a coloured bar above the plots
Fig 5 legend: "recordings from during verses before stimulation" : Unclear what is meant here.
P12. first para: "red 4 × 4 array (~12 mW/mm2) simultaneously" : This power information should also be written for the above
experiments.
p14, first para: "frequency bins exhibiting significant (Bonferroni correction applied to p < 0.05) modulation from stimulation".
I don’t remember seeing a multiple comparison correction for the previous analysis in Fig 4. And is the highly restrictive
Bonferroni the most appropriate correction for this study? I personally prefer FDR correction for those analyses.
No in-text reference to Fig 7A-C
Fig 7: Please add references to onset/ of reaches in the plot.
p15, first para: "and efficient viral vector delivery without live-MRI monitoring" It’s not clear how this technology enables
doing a CED injection without MRI. Could anyone just stick a needle inside a craniotomy and inject CED, even without this
platform? If your technology assists with needle placement and stability, or reflux monitoring, then I think it is a better selling
point.
p16, first para: "with traditional window-less approaches, like Utah arrays" I recommend citing the latest Angelucci Opto-
Utah Array paper.
", is much more challenging in comparison to our window-based method. " I am not sure this is a fair comparison. I can think
of several ways in which a fully closed approach is safer and easier… (e.g. infection risks, human translation). Maybe the
main selling point of your approach is the constant visualization and monitoring, including with ephys, of the tested sites?
p16, 4th para: "Early works attempting to integrate electrode arrays and large-scale optical windows did not result in long-
term optical access " I would like to see data about pressure on the cortex caused by the window, and related depression,
as shown in Yazdan, Neuron 2016. Has this been resolved?.
I also do not see any histological data in this paper. I assume the NHPs are still alive and performing tasks? Previous papers
from this group included much useful histological verification. This would be even more useful in this case given the strange
behavior of the Jaws opsin on ephys (excitation rather than inhibition, positive effects even on non-transduced sites).
Thoughts: Jaws is a very sensitive opsin. Could the positive effects even on non-transduced sites be a result of stimulation
of nearby transduced sites by distant LEDs? Even a small amount of light could trigger those distant sites, and through
network effects, influence ephys readings at the stimulated, non-transduced site? Is it possible to run some tests in a non-
injected monkey?
Is it also possible that epifluorescence is not a perfect indicator of transduced vs non-transduced sites? Maybe at sites where
epifluorescence is not visible (at the threshold used), there are still a number of neurons or axon terminals expressing the
Jaws opsin?
Overall, great study combining cutting edge optogenetics and clever hardware developments that are much needed to boost
causal, cell-type specific neuro research in the primate brain. Looking forward to the revised paper.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Griggs et al. presents a cost-effective and scalable platform capable of multimodal optogenetic and
neurophysiological studies in behaving macaques positioned in a primate chair. In contrast to other published macaque
chamber-mounted systems, the key advances of this platform include its scalability, the integration of LFP/ECoG capabilities
into the artificial dura (the MMAD), and its ability to perform patterned optogenetic stimulation. The authors demonstrate the
system’s functionality by showcasing its capability to monitor epifluorescence (optogenetic expression) over several months,
as well as its ability to modulate LPFs and reaching behavior through optogenetic stimulation. I commend the authors for
acknowledging that the clear view of the brain through the artificial dura typically lasts only a couple of months, after which a
tissue removal procedure is required to regain visual access for further studies. While this limitation, along with others (e.g.,
risk of infection, optogenetic light artifacts in neurophysiological signals, and the focus on surface-level recordings),
constrains its ability to fully reveal the circuitry underlying behavior, the utilization of this platform can set the stage for
significant advancements in primate cognitive neuroscience.
Major Comments
(1) Reproducibility of results across days is not addressed in the manuscript. This is true for (a)
epifluorescence, since only the collection but not quantitation was described in the Star Methods; (b) consistency of the
optical window, since alignment procedures for the FOV, blood vessel changes across days and weeks (e.g. Figure 3 top row)
were not discussed; (c) LFP signals, in Figure 4 it is unclear as to the sample size of the LFP data (e.g. number of trials),
let alone whether it was collected across multiple days or weeks); (d) behavioral measures, how consistence were the effects
of optogenetic stimulation on behavior across days.
(2) Information provided in Supp Figure 5 on the removal of light-induced artifact should be promoted to the main manuscript.
With modeling, could the onset 50ms and offset 50ms LFP, discarded in subsequent analyses, be recovered as suggested
by Supp Figure 5D?
(3) A briefer summary of the behavioral results (Figure 6). Reducing even further the behavioral data would help focus the
manuscript onto the device. Actually, once the behavioral data was introduced, this reader was looking for a more in-depth
analysis and interpretation of those results (as well as wondering about the next obvious experiments that must have been
performed) than that provided in the manuscript and supplemental materials. For instance, examining the effects on behavior
of varying the pattern targeting different functional cortical areas (or amplitude or duration or timing) of optogenetic
stimulation would have really brought home the utility of the large-scale platform.
(4) With the usage of the term ‘optical imaging’ this reader expected that functional intrinsic optical imaging would be one of
the major modalities of this large-scale platform. Instead, what is advanced here is visual access to the surface of the brain
under the term of ‘optical imaging’. The authors should clarify this distinction early on and suggest (e.g., in the Discussion)
that intrinsic optical imaging, combined with behavioral studies, is feasible with the current platform—though without the
other modalities, as the hardware for those may interfere with intrinsic optical imaging.
Moderate and Minor Comments:
(1) Figure 1D. Please provide a mm scale bar to Figure 1D. This will provide to the reader a good reference of the sizes of the
outside of the chamber and area of surface of the brain available for study. This will also allow the reader to appreciate the
space dedicated to store the ECOG cabling.
(2) The assembly of the LED array was designed to minimize conductive heating of the brain. However, the manuscript did
not report the actual heat transfer with typical full array LED stimulation through the cover glass or through the MMAD,
gauging the success of these efforts. Thus it is unclear whether without obvious airflow that an Air Gap was effective.
(3) The manuscript reports chamber stability for 2-3 years, with MMAD re-implantations for additional experiments. However,
it is unclear if the chamber remains in use or has been removed. Clarifying whether the chamber is still in use or has been
removed would help the reader understand the platform’s longevity and suitability for even longer-term studies.
(4) Figure 4. Upon printout (this reviewer still works with hard copy), the small font size of Figure 4 was unreadable. Please
reformat Figure 4 so it can be reproduced nicely on the printed page.
(5) Results related to Figure 4. Data from Monkey L. How many ECoG sites were included in this data set? Were both opsin
expressing and opsin deficient sites included? How many stimulation trails were included? Were similar findings obtained
from Monkey H. May I recommend reporting the statistics throughout the manuscript using the APA Style Guidelines.
(6) Results related to Figure 4D. The manuscript reports a red LED energy of ~12 mW/mm2, but does not report the energy
directed towards the brain for either the red laser or blue (485 nm) LED. Without information on the Blue LEDs and the
absorption spectrum of the JAWs opsin for these two wavelengths, it is difficult for the reader to assess whether the
differences in PSD power observed in Figure 4D are smaller than expected based on theoretical modeling. In other words, it
is unclear whether or not the blue LED sub-optimally drives the JAWs opsin.
(7) Results related to Figure 4G-O. The Spectrograms show an increase in activity during the 900 ms after stimulation offset
relative to the 500 ms of pre-stimulus activity. This apparently interesting long-lasting effect of stimulation though shown in
Figure 4D was not discussed in the Results. Also, what is the authors’ interpretation of the relatively uniform increase in
activity across frequencies?
(8) Results related to Figure 4I. The Frequency spectrogram suggests the duration of laser stimulation lasted about 150 ms
longer than the targeted 900 ms for the LEDs. Could this have happened? If not, the authors should make an account for the
laser eliciting a longer lasting response than the LED.
(9) Results related to Figure 4D-E-F. The Median PSD Ratio y-axis scale is not linear (and not a standard log scale);
whereas the Power ratio is graphed linearly in Figure 5CD. Is that non-linearity intended? If yes, what is that scaling?
(10) Results related to Figure 4E-F. The 95% CI of the medians in some instances fall below a ratio of 1. Is this valid?
(11) Results related to Figure 4 (and Figure 5 data). What was the interstimulus interval?
(12) Figure 5. Legend title: “Map of neural responses…” is inaccurate as the locations of the ECoG recordings are not shown
(as in Supp Figure 2).
(13) Results related to Figure 5CD. How many trials and ECoG sites were used to generate these graphs, and over what
time period? Additionally, in this figure, the whiskers represent the standard error of the mean, while in Figure 4, whiskers
represent 95% confidence intervals. What is the reason for this inconsistency between Figures?
(14) Behavioral task. What was the size of the target windows and distance in cm between the start and end targets? Maybe
add a cm scale bar to Figure 6A, B, or C.
(15) Behavioral task. The reporting of some of the statistical results might be questioned. For instance, this reader questions
the validity of reporting the last decimal places of some of the values. For example, ‘total: p = 0.0001560’, should the reader
place any credence in the last ‘560’ or is that just a computer output without validation of the number of significant digits that
should validly be reported? Again, may I recommend reporting the statistics according to APA Style Guidelines.
(16) Results related to Figure 6. Given the focus of the manuscript, this Figure in this reader’s opinion seemed a little overkill
and difficult to interpret during the presentation of the Reach Times (Figure 6F-G). Since Path Lengths (Figure 6D) and reach
onsets seem to be the major variables affected by optogenetic stimulation, maybe just present those results in the main
manuscript.
(17) Results related to Figure 6. “Whiskers are described as representing the standard error of the mean, and asterisks
denote p < 0.05 using a Mann-Whitney U-test”. Since the Mann-Whitney U-test is a non-parametric test used to assess
significant differences between two independent, non-normally distributed groups, why are means, rather than medians and
confidence intervals, presented in the graphs? Alternatively, if the data groups are normally distributed, why weren’t t-tests
employed instead?
(18) Results related to Figure 7. Again, how many trials and ECoG sites were used to generate the graphs in panels D and
H? The whiskers are described as representing 95% confidence intervals of the average, but they appear quite small for
95% CIs. Is this correct? Additionally, why was there a switch to a.u. for Average Power? If th reason for this was mentioned
in the manuscript, it may have been unclear to this reader.
(19) The manuscript’s usage of ‘slow reach’ reads awkwardly to this reader. My general interpretation of this word pairing is
that the actual movement is slower (e.g., like a sloth). Instead, based on the presentation of the results it appears (but I could
be mistaken) that reach onset and reach trajectory lengths were affected by the optogenetic stimulation (and not movement
velocity). Thus the usage of ‘slow reach’ is not ideal.
(20) The manuscript emphasizes that previously published CED protocols relied on MRI to monitor infusions, whereas this is
not required with the current platform. However, aside from visual inspection of the surface, there is a noticeable lack of
subsequent monitoring of CED infusion, as indicated by the few failed attempts reported. In this reader’s opinion, this
difference in the CED protocol is relatively minor and does not represent a significant advancement as advocated for in the
manuscript (I would tone that down).
(21) Discussion. The manuscript reports an unexpected increase in ECoG power during optogenetic stimulation with an
inhibitory opsin. A more in-depth discussion of possible reasons for this observation is warranted. Similarly, given the
behavioral results, a more in-depth discussion on these outcomes would be anticipated given the suspected roles of area 5
and area 7 in reaching behavior.
(22) Discussion. Upon a single reading, it seemed to this reviewer that there were sentences/paragraphs in the Discussion
that were nearly identical to those written either in the Introduction or Results. Please revise/edit accordingly to reduce such
repetition.
(23) Supp Figure 2D. Again, why was a Mann-Whitney U-test used if means and standard errors are being graphed (see
previous comment)? Again, how many trials and ECoG sites were used to generate these graphs? Graphing such small
standard errors is far less informative to the reader than 95% confidence intervals would be. Were similar findings seen for
Monkey H?
(24) Supp Figure 3. Am I correct in assuming the results for the 4-arrow symbol (top row) is the vector sum of the individual
reach directions (next 4 rows)? If that assumption is true, then for Monkey H for the y-dimension there appears to be
something way off. Same for Monkey L.
(25) Supp Figure 5. Shouldn’t Suppl Figure 5 E-F lower graphs (after artifact removal) be identical to graphs Figure 7E and
Figure 7F? They are similar but also different in visually significant ways, even when one takes into account the different
scale for Suppl Figure 5F.
(26) Supp Fig 5A: What was the source of the LFP time courses (n=13)? Were they from a single animal, a single trial, or
averaged over multiple trials? What was the experimental session type, and were the time courses located over opsin-
expressing or opsin-deficient sites? Additionally, for all the analysese, were certain ECoG sites preferentially included or
excluded, and if so, what criteria were used for selection? Finally, was the goodness of fit of the regression used to evaluate
the effectiveness of photo-induced artifact removal for individual ECoG sites?
(27) Supp Fig 5C. Please also show the ‘fit’ during the after-stimulation period as well.
(28) Figure 6 and Supp Fig 3: Given the large number of null hypotheses tested, there is a risk of Type 1 statistical errors.
Please ensure appropriate corrections are applied to account for multiple comparisons.
Typos:
1. Page 4, line 31: “center-our reach task” – should be “center-out reach task”.
2. Page 10, line 25: "it’s compatibility with lasers" –should be "its".
3. StarMethods: Resister – should be resistor?
4. StarMethods: “Christ Instruments” – should be” Crist Instrument Company”.
5. Term ‘LED’ is not defined.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents a comprehensive account of a large-scale optogenetic neurophysiology platform designed for non-
human primates (NHP) and illustrates its application in a behavioral study. While the organization and clarity of the
manuscript are commendable, I have considerable reservations about the novelty and scientific importance of this work,
particularly in relation to its potential publication in Nature Communications.
One of the main challenges facing optogenetics in primate research is the effective outcome of behavioral manipulation,
especially regarding motor actions. In its current form, the study utilizing the assembled platform does not significantly
advance this field. Although it shows some impact on reaching behaviors, I question the practicality of the platform as
presented, regardless of its apparent complexity.
Furthermore, if the objective is to utilize this device for exploring the neural mechanisms behind specific cognitive functions
or understanding network dynamics, the existing design offers no distinct advantages over current technologies. The ECoG
array is limited to capturing local field potentials, and the extensive LED array suffers from inadequate spatial resolution and
substantial interference artifacts. Together, these limitations render the system less appealing.
To enhance the design, I propose the following suggestions:
1. Consider replacing the LED array with a micro-LED array to improve spatial resolution (doi.org/10.1038/s41592-021-
01238-9). This micro-LED array could be programmed for high temporal resolution, theoretically producing lower artifacts
and thereby increasing the likelihood of capturing transient changes in neural activity. Additionally, implementing an LED
array with dual wavelengths could facilitate simultaneous activation and deactivation using one device.
2. I recommend mapping the finger and arm zones prior to light stimulation. Random stimulation tends to be less effective in
eliciting behavioral responses. I encourage the authors to adopt a different strategy: record neural activity during reaching
tasks across a broad cortical area, and subsequently program the micro-LED array to illuminate the brain in alignment with
the recorded activation patterns. Given that these patterns will vary in both space and time, mastering the programming of
the LED array is crucial.
Specific concerns include:
1. I find the rationale behind the unexpected increase in ECoG signals unconvincing. A straightforward verification could be
conducted through single-unit recordings.
2. Although the authors conducted control experiments to indicate that responses were largely optogenetically induced, they
were unable to completely eliminate the thermal effects. Therefore, an additional control trial involving non-expressing
monkeys (or the same monkey before viral injection) remains necessary. While I acknowledge the associated challenges,
the experiment, as it stands, lacks thoroughness.
Typos:
line 94: accessibly->accessibility
line 112: center-our->center-out

### Reviewer 4

Griggs and colleagues present an integrated optogenetic and electrocorticography (ECoG) platform designed for use in
macaques. This is an impressive technical achievement, combining optogenetic modulation with large-scale neural
recordings. While similar techniques have been proposed individually or with more complex approaches, this tool seems
relatively straightforward to implement in a lab with enough technical expertise. I highly commend the authors for developing
and utilizing such an innovative piece of technology. I’m convinced many will be interested in these tools.
However, I find myself less convinced by the neuroscientific aspects of the manuscript. As the authors themselves highlight,
it is puzzling to observe a net increase in LFP power following Jaws stimulation. While optogenetic stimulation with a
hyperpolarizing opsin is known to induce a mixture of inhibitory and excitatory effects at the single-unit level, population-
level effects should generally lead to net inhibition. The weak behavioral effects observed also suggest that the output of the
stimulated region might be slightly reduced, which contradicts the observed increase in LFP power. In my view, this
unexpected result warrants further explanation and exploration. Given the substantial light-induced artifacts observed in
saline (Fig. S5), I am still uncertain whether these effects are truly neuronal, despite the authors’ counter-arguments.
I was surprised that the authors averaged their results across all ECoG channels (Fig. 4 G-O; 7). Surely, in Figure 5, they
distinguish between transduced and non-transduced sectors. I recommend that they apply a similar analysis based on the
functional properties of the cortex under the electrodes. For example, by using task-induced neuronal activity (such as
reaching-related activity) from both transduced and non-transduced areas, they could define regions of interest (ROIs)
across 4 different cortical regions (transduced or not, functionally relevant or not). This would allow for a more refined
analysis of the data.
Moreover, it would be valuable to replicate these experiments using a penetrating electrode (e.g., a laminar probe) to
compare the surprising ECoG data with single- or multi-unit recordings, providing additional insight into the neuronal effects.
In summary, this is a highly interesting technical paper that somehow should be published, but I believe it should be
considered for its methodological contributions rather than its neuroscientific conclusions. As such, I am presently
unconvinced it is suitable for publication in Nature Communications. IMHO, a more thorough investigation of the neuronal
and behavioral effects (see below) is warranted, but I refrain to the editors to make that call.
Minor Comments:
1. Method Limitations: The authors highlight the advantages of their new method but should also mention its limitations. For
example, the method is limited to recording from superficial, easily accessible parts of the cortex and cannot capture data
from structures buried in sulci or from deeper cortical areas that are not accessible with the current setup. Surely, more
limitations can be listed.
2. Neuronal Data with Dura Resection: The authors mention that their MMAD allows recording for 10-14 weeks, after which
dura growth requires resection. While stability of GFP expression is clearly illustrated in Figure 3, it would be informative to
include raw neuronal traces for the same periods, along with both GFP and neuronal data after multiple dura resections
(e.g., approximately 2-3 years post-implant).
3. Figure 3C: This figure requires more explanation. It is unclear what point the authors are trying to make, and further
clarification would be helpful.
4. Figure 4: The fonts and arrowheads in this figure are barely visible. Please increase their size for better clarity.
5. Figure 4 Statistical Analysis: I suspect the statistics in Figure 4 use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. It is unusual to observe
significant changes in the pre-stimulation period. Was a correction for multiple comparisons applied? If not, this should be
done. If a correction was applied, could the authors explain the pre-stimulation differences?
6. Non-Neuronal Effects: The authors argue that the ECoG responses are “primarily” optogenetically evoked (non-thermal).
However, control experiments indicate substantial non-neuronal effects. Can the authors estimate the contributions of these
two effects (neuronal vs. non-neuronal) to the observed in vivo data?
7. Behavioral Data Statistical Analysis: Was a correction for multiple comparisons applied to the behavioral data? If not, I
suggest this be done to ensure the robustness of the results.
8. Spatially-Specific Behavioral Effects: I was surprised by the lack of consistent spatially-specific behavioral effects. How
reliable were these effects across sessions or across trial blocks within the same session? Test-retest reliability should be
shown to strengthen the findings.
9. Figure 6 Significance Indicators: The asterisks indicating significance in Figure 6 do not always match the descriptions in
the text. Please check for accuracy. Were all trials included in the analysis for this figure?
10. Figure 7: As mentioned earlier, it would be highly informative to show time-frequency plots for four different electrode
sites (transduced vs. non-transduced and task-modulated vs. non-task-modulated sites).
11. Interpretation of Reaching Behavior: The authors interpret the stimulation-induced changes in reaching behavior as
changes in motor dynamics. However, this region of the parietal cortex is involved in a variety of interrelated functions,
including but not restricted to e.g. attention, multisensory integration, and decision-making. How do the authors disentangle
these contributions from the motor changes observed in the reaching task?

### Reviewer 5

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications.

You previously reviewed this paper and raised several concerns. The authors have now submitted a revised manuscript along with a detailed point-by-point response. Your task is to write your updated review after carefully reading:
  1. The revised paper
  2. Your original Round 1 review
  3. The authors' point-by-point response

In your updated review, explicitly state which concerns have been adequately addressed and which remain outstanding. Be specific.

## Paper

## Abstract

Optogenetics has been a powerful scientific tool for two decades, yet its integration with non-human primate (NHP) electrophysiology has been limited due to several technical challenges. These include a lack of electrode arrays capable of supporting large-scale and long-term optical access, inaccessible viral vector delivery methods for transfection of large regions of cortex, a paucity of hardware designed for large-scale patterned cortical illumination, and limited designs for multi-modal experimentation. To address these gaps, we introduce a highly accessible platform integrating optogenetics and electrophysiology for behavioral and neural modulation with neurophysiological recording in NHPs. We employed this platform in two rhesus macaques and showcased its capability of optogenetically disrupting reaches, while simultaneously monitoring ongoing electrocorticography activity underlying the stimulation-induced behavioral changes. The platform exhibits long-term stability and functionality, thereby facilitating large-scale electrophysiology, optical imaging, and optogenetics over months, which is crucial for translationally relevant multi-modal studies of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.

---

## Introduction

Optogenetics is unique among neuromodulation technologies because it allows for cell-type-specific manipulation of neural networks with high spatial and temporal precision. This enables the precise manipulations needed for research in fundamental neuroscience1–5, such as investigating relationships between neural activity and behavior4–8, monitoring changes in neural circuitry over time7,9, understanding the neural changes associated with brain dysfunction10,11 and developing therapies for neurological disorders1,3,5,12,13.

The evolutionary proximity between the neurophysiology of non-human primates (NHPs) and humans14–16 spurs us to apply optogenetics to NHPs to better understand the human brain and strengthen translational medical research, especially in the context of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders. However, studying neurological disease models in NHPs is challenging because NHP neuropathology and anomalous neural activity are often spatiotemporally complex, spanning multiple brain areas and months or years of development, much like in humans. These challenges, along with the scientific opportunities afforded by optogenetics, call for the development of large-scale, chronically stable optogenetic platforms for NHPs.

Although the development of optogenetic techniques in NHPs emerged soon after the debut of optogenetics17,18, its wide-spread adoption has remained a challenge. We dissect key contributing factors below that are addressed in our platform.

While optogenetics alone is a potent technique for functional neuropathological studies, the integration of optogenetics with an electrical platform, such as electrocorticography (ECoG) recordings, can enable precise optical control over specific cell types with concurrent measurement of neural activity at high spatiotemporal resolution. Merging of optogenetic and electrical recording platforms has been demonstrated in rodent work19,20, however, similar attempts in NHP work have come with limitations. Systems where skin is closed over the implant require surgeries for device replacements or modifications and prevent ongoing assessment of both optical occlusions between the light source and the brain, as well as optogenetic expression21, which is typically confirmed with optical techniques. Such limitations make these systems experimentally inflexible.

In contrast, modular chambers enabling chronic access to the cortical surface have been developed. In particular, in vivo optical imaging of NHP brains through cranial windows has been a small but vibrant field with decades of development with techniques such as calcium imaging22, voltage-sensitive dyes23,24, intrinsic signal optical imaging24,25, and epifluoresence imaging9,26, among others. Optical windows to the NHP brain are often covered with a transparent, silicone-based artificial dura to protect the brain while providing optical access to the cortex23–26. The artificial dura has been combined with optical stimulation methods such as infrared neural stimulation27 and optogenetics25,28. In a previous effort, we have taken a similar approach and performed simultaneous electrical recording and optogenetic stimulation using a µECoG array in an optical window. However, long-term optical access stability using this approach remained an unmet challenge. One approach relied on daily explantation of an artificial dura and implantation of a µECoG array to perform experiments, but the frequent manipulation of the cortical surface stimulated tissue growth over the cortex and obscured optical access26,29. Another approach relied on chronic co-implantation of both an artificial dura and a µECoG array between the artificial dura and the brain, but tissue growth between the artificial dura and the µECoG array obscured optical access29,30. To take full advantage of optogenetics in NHPs, there is a need for innovative platforms with chronic stability in both electrophysiology and optical access to empower widespread adoption.

One obstacle in NHP optogenetics, not present in rodent models, is the size of NHP brains, which renders widespread viral delivery of optogenetic vectors impractical via traditional, diffusion-based methods. In contrast, convection-enhanced delivery (CED) is a pressure-based approach of infusion allowing for large-scale and even distribution of viral expression in comparison to diffusion-based approaches26,31. Previously published CED protocols relied on live magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to monitor infusions26,32, making these methods technically challenging and only accessible to the institutions capable of MRI-guided viral infusions in the NHP brain.

Given the challenges of attaining large-scale optogenetic coverage and maintaining optical access, large-scale optical stimulation techniques have been largely undeveloped—optogenetic stimulation in NHPs is generally performed by fiber optics or optrodes coupled to lasers33, which are not optimized for large-area optogenetic coverage. Light emitting diode (LED) arrays, both with21 and without34,35 simultaneous electrophysiological recording, have also been used, but with limited cortical coverage or access. Optogenetic transduction and stimulation methods, that are both experimentally flexible and widely accessible, are necessary to capitalize on large-scale optogenetics in NHPs.

In this paper, we address the above challenges by designing accessible tools and integrating them into a single platform. We demonstrate large-scale, chronically stable optogenetics and ECoG in an imaging window on NHP cortex. We present an optogenetic platform comprised of five complementary state-of-the-art technological advancements, enhancing both experimental flexibility and accessibility to researchers with diverse technical backgrounds. Our advancements are: (1) a platform designed to be modular and flexible for varied, multi-modal use-cases; (2) a chronically implanted integration of an ECoG array and an artificial dura, which we refer to as a multi-modal artificial dura (MMAD); (3) optical hardware scalable from single lasers up to large arrays of LEDs for complex patterned stimulation across multiple brain areas; (4) improved ECoG-compatible optical access with the MMAD, facilitating long-term multi-modal experimentation; and (5) CED without live-MRI guidance, which is an accessible viral vector delivery method for achieving large-scale expression. These technologies are synergistic yet maintain functional modularity, i.e., no one technology requires all the others to function, thus keeping our platform relevant for experiments requiring fewer than our full suite of technologies, while maintaining forward compatibility. Our work is poised to bridge the gap between rodents and humans by facilitating powerful, multi-modal studies in NHPs.

We demonstrated the efficacy of our advancements by three complimentary measures: optical imaging, electrophysiology, and behavior. We present months of continuous optical clarity with the MMAD and years of chamber stability, which open opportunities for translational studies of models of neurological diseases and disorders such as stroke recovery36. The optical clarity empowered verification of large-scale epifluorescence, the product of our viral delivery process, and our ECoG recordings confirmed the flexibility of our scalable optical stimulation setup for optogenetic experimentation. We demonstrated our platform’s relevance for behavioral studies by optogenetically disrupting a center-out reach task by modulating the posterior parietal cortex (PPC). This showcases the applicability of our platform for complex behavioral experiments. This work provides a milestone proof-of-concept for NHP behavior experiments with inhibitory opsins which, up to this point, have not been successfully applied to reaching behavior.

The ability to link millisecond-resolution neural activity with behavioral effects and optogenetic neuronal manipulation is an invaluable addition to the NHP researcher’s toolbox. Therefore, we took measures to ensure the accessibility of our methods for a diverse range of specialties: design files are provided for parts and equipment that are not commercially available, our in-house fabrication processes require only generic equipment and modest skill, and our neural processing code is publicly available. Collectively, our work enables large-scale and long-term interrogation of cortical areas in awake behaving NHPs37,38.

---

## Results

Hardware
We designed and implemented our platform for two healthy adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta, Monkeys H and L). We used magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based methods to plan a craniotomy with a diameter (Ø) of 25 mm over the left PPC and to design a custom chamber with a curvature precisely fitting the surface of the skull around the craniotomy for each monkey (Fig. 1a, c). We have previously published these methods as step-by-step protocols for accessibility39,40. The custom chamber was designed to provide a sturdy base for experimental equipment and protect the brain when the monkey is freely moving between experiments. The chamber is further described in Methods. We implanted the chamber along with our multi-modal artificial dura (MMAD; Fig. 1b, d41;) in both animals. The chambers continue to be stable and used for studies after >4.6 and >3.8 years following implantation for Monkeys H and L, respectively, and we have not observed behavioral or health deficits.

We designed the MMAD to serve both as an optical window to the brain and as an electrocorticography (ECoG) array. The MMAD is composed of a flexible and corrosion-resistant electrode array molded in silicone into a “top-hat” shape common for traditional artificial duras40,42. The opaque, conductive traces of the MMAD are layered on top of each other to maximize the optical access to the brain through the transparent polymer of the MMAD41. Like traditional artificial duras, the MMAD protects the brain and keeps the brain moist during experiments. Unlike traditional artificial duras, cables extend from the “top-hat” of the MMAD to hardware for electrophysiological recordings, as described below. We packaged the MMAD cables inside the chamber between experiments (Fig. 1d). The MMAD, as well as the commercially available electrode array (Ripple Neuro, Salt Lake City, UT) from which the MMAD was fabricated, are further described in Methods.

The MMAD cables require adapters, called clamp connectors, to be used with external electrophysiology equipment. We designed a stack-up of parts to attach to the chamber and support the clamp connectors (Fig. 1e, f). All parts are designed to be modular for flexible experimentation and design iterations as needed. Further descriptions of parts can be found in Methods, and design files are publicly available (see Data and Code Availability).

We designed and tested our platform for both laser- and LED-based optical stimulation. The lasers and optical fibers were commercially sourced and can support a variety of light wavelengths (see Methods for further laser system details). We designed an LED array and its driving circuitry in-house (Fig. 2, Supplementary Fig. 1) to be compatible with high temporal resolution (sub-millisecond) requirements (Supplementary Movie 1). While pulse-width modulation is a popular technique for driving LEDs, we designed our driving circuitry to be controlled by analog signals. Specifically, we drove our LEDs with continuous voltage signals to avoid high-frequency photo-induced artifacts in our electrophysiology recordings. We selected LEDs for optimal tissue penetration and powered our circuitry with two rechargeable 9V batteries to mitigate line noise (Supplementary Fig. 1). We designed and fabricated two versions of an LED array for patterned stimulation, a 4 × 4 array with individually drivable LED columns43. and a 3 × 5 array with independently drivable LEDs (Fig. 2a). An example stimulation pattern demonstrating spatial, temporal, and optical power complexity is provided (Supplementary Movie 1). Both boards used identical schematics for the driving circuitry except for the number of LEDs driven by each driving circuit (Supplementary Fig. 1). We fabricated our LED arrays in two wavelengths (634 nm and 485 nm). The LED array was protected from potential moisture from the brain by a cover glass between the LED array and the MMAD (Figs. 1e–g, 2b). This also provided a small air gap between the LEDs and the cover glass to mitigate conductive heating of the brain (Fig. 2b). Our benchtop temperature measurement data indicate our stimulation design limits the cortical temperature change to less than 1 °C during our stimulation protocols (Supplementary Fig. 2), which is below the safe limit for brain44–47 and has minimal impact on neuronal activity48,49. We did not observe any tissue damage (e.g., brain discoloration) or behavioral deficits over the years in our animals.

We commercially sourced our custom printed circuit boards (PCBs) and assembled the LED array and driver PCBs in-house with common soldering methods. (For more details, see Methods).

Optical stability
To demonstrate the stability of optical access through the MMAD we used both optical epifluorescence imaging and stimulation. With our MMAD, we achieved 10 to 14 consecutive weeks of optical access in our monkeys before tissue growth began to obstruct light penetration (Supplementary Fig. 3). After tissue had matured, we resected the tissue and reimplanted the MMAD for additional experiments.

As aforementioned, both implanted monkeys have been stable for ~4 years following surgery, and the chambers have supported optical experiments, displaying the platform’s ability to facilitate long-term NHP studies. Over this period, we have repeated the dura resection and reimplantation of the MMAD for both monkeys, each allowing us windows of >10 weeks of optical access for experimentation. In some instances, we observed accelerated tissue growth when we explanted the MMAD to test other recording and stimulation systems. For example, following a tissue resection in Monkey H approximately two years after first implantation, the MMAD was replaced and clear optical access was maintained for 7 weeks. At week 7, while optical access was still clear, the MMAD was removed to test other stimulation and recording devices that impacted tissue growth. Approximately one week later, tissue began to grow over the cortex. For another example, one and a half years after the first implantation in Monkey L, a similar procedure provided clear optical access for at least 5.5 weeks during which we ran experiments. Similarly, the MMAD was removed for another experiment that led to tissue growth. These results collectively show the stability of optical access with our design for several months and the modularity of our platform to test other recording and stimulation devices. In addition, our results caution that explantation and implantation of the MMAD must be minimized, because it is known that mechanical manipulation on the surface of the brain causes irritation of the cortical surface and can lead to accelerated tissue growth that obscures optical access.

CED during chamber implantation surgery, we used CED (similar to9,26,50,51) to infuse up to 50 µL of a pan-neuronal inhibitory optogenetic viral vector (AAV8-hSyn-Jaws-GFP, 5.4 × 1012 genome copies per milliliter (gc/mL))52,53 at several locations across the craniotomy (Fig. 3). We delivered viral vector at rates up to 5 µL/min using our custom-built stepped-tip cannula26. Further descriptions of parts, equipment, and protocols are provided in Methods.

We infused the optogenetic viral vector in the surgery suite immediately prior to chamber implantation. This allowed us to visually inspect any potential reflux on the surface of the brain from the cannula without live-MRI, which we had used in previous protocols. For our presented protocol, we had eleven successful and two unsuccessful infusions as determined by epifluorescent expression near the locations of cannula insertion. We canceled one infusion before its completion because the brain did not seal against the cannula and we observed fluid buildup, likely reflux (Fig. 3c, d). We reattempted that infusion nearby and successfully generated expression (Fig. 3d). In the first surgery (Monkey H), we had difficulty determining the depth of cannula penetration into the brain with stereotactic instruments alone because of the brain’s tendency to dimple during cannula insertion. To address this in our second surgery (Monkey L), we marked the cannula prior to surgery at a set distance distal from the cannula’s tip to facilitate measurement of penetration depth during surgery. This technique correlated with an improvement in success rate between our first and second surgeries (62% and 100%, respectively; Fig. 3c, d).

Our long-term and large-scale optical access provided by the MMAD empowered us to monitor optogenetic expression over time for both monkeys. Monkey H underwent initial imaging for epifluorescence two weeks after viral infusion. Expression was evident during the first imaging session and increased in coverage and intensity until the fifth week after infusion, when expression plateaued at 92 mm2 coverage (Fig. 3b, d). Similarly, we confirmed 76 mm2 expression coverage in Monkey L (Fig. 3d). Although we did not see a change in epifluorescent expression during the initial months following the plateau in viral expression area, approximately two years after infusion we observed a strong reduction of expression in both monkeys.

Photo-induced artifact removal
Our optical stimulation system generated artifacts in the ECoG data. To remove artifacts from ECoG data, we generated a dataset of artifacts, in the absence of any neural signals, by optically stimulating an MMAD submerged in a saline bath. We modeled the photo-induced artifact using these saline data, fit the model to the in vivo ECoG data, and removed the estimated photo-induced artifact (see Methods for details). The results demonstrate that the method effectively removes photo-induced artifacts (Fig. 4a). As a control, we tested the artifact removal method on data without stimulation and found that the method had negligible effect, as intended (Fig. 4b, c).

Stimulation at rest
To demonstrate our platform’s ability to integrate optogenetics and ECoG, we applied optical stimulation protocols (Fig. 5a, b) and recorded evoked neural activity. We removed photo-induced artifact as described above and in Methods. Statistical tests were run by comparing the neural activity to the baseline recording before the onset of stimulation (Bonferroni correction applied to p < 0.05).

We stimulated an opsin-expressing area of Monkey L during rest with one of the red LEDs of the 3 × 5 LED array (634 nm, 75 mW, 900 ms; Fig. 5a). The stimulation produced a significant increase in ECoG power across most frequencies and weaker effects persisted after the end of stimulation (Fig. 5a, c, e) probably due to spatiotemporal complexities of neural networks, including the possibly of rebound effects54. The effects of stimulation were similar but weaker at nearby electrodes (Fig. 5a, c, g, i) (0 mm vs 2 mm p = 7.7e–6, 0 mm vs 2 mm p = 4.6e−8). In addition to testing our LED array, we also tested traditional laser stimulation. We stimulated neural tissue of Monkey L with fiber optic cable connected to a laser (638 nm, 45 mW, 900 ms; Fig. 5b). Again, the stimulation produced a significant increase in ECoG power across high frequencies and weaker effects persisted after the end of stimulation (Fig. 5b, d, f). However, the persisting effects were more pronounced than with LED stimulation, likely due to the focal nature of collimated laser stimulation as opposed to the less focal, uncollimated LED stimulation. Effects were primarily local (Fig. 5b, d, f, h, j), which aligned with our expectation that laser stimulation would have a more focal effect than LED stimulation (0 mm vs 2 mm p = 5.5e−7, 0 mm vs 4 mm p = 1.2e−6). A similar experiment with Monkey H produced similar results (Supplementary Fig. 4).

However, we expected that inhibitory optogenetics would cause ECoG power to decrease in general, not increase. To validate the light-evoked responses observed, we have performed a series of control experiments described below.

We investigated the spatial nature of the neural responses with respect to opsin-expressing and opsin deficient areas (Fig. 6). To test the spatial nature of the neural responses, we stimulated all 16 red LEDs of the 4 × 4 array (634 nm, ~12 mW/mm2) during rest and separated recording channels based on the expression in their vicinity. A control animal, Monkey C, which had never been genetically altered, did not show statistically significant changes in neural activity (p = 0.53; Fig. 6d). For both optogenetic monkeys, ECoG power evoked by red LEDs was statistically stronger in the opsin expressing areas than the opsin deficient areas (Monkey H: p = 0.012; Monkey L: p = 8.3e−9; Fig. 6a, c). We repeated the experiment with sub-optimal stimulation techniques in Monkey L, being red LED stimulation with tissue growth over the brain and blue (485 nm) LED stimulation of a clear window, and found there was no significant difference between the opsin expressing and opsin deficient areas (tissue p = 0.47; blue light p = 0.90; Fig. 6c). Responses when optical access was clear produced significantly higher power in opsin expressing areas compared to conditions of tissue growth and the use of blue light (tissue p = 1.8e−4, blue p = 3.0e−59). Repeating the red light stimulation experiment with the full LED array and clear optical access in Monkey H ~2 years after initial infusion, when most of the epifluorescence had dissipated, produced no statistically significant changes from natural fluctuations in a baseline activity without optical stimulation (p = 0.76; Fig. 6b).

Comparing light-evoked responses from opsin expressing and opsin deficient regions across days yielded statistically significant differences in Monkey L (Fig. 6e). Note that after 540 days for monkey L and 686 days for monkey H we saw decreased expression as measured by both epifluorescence and insignificant light-evoked responses (H: p = 0.89, L: p = 0.92; Fig. 6e, f). We then reinjected 838 days after initial injection in Monkey L and 1,435 days after in initial injection in Monkey H (Fig. 6e, f) and generated approximately the same stimulation-evoked activity levels as the first injection in both opsin expressing and opsin deficient areas although with smaller expression regions (Fig. 6e, f). Collectively, the differences between light-evoked responses of opsin expression and opsin deficient regions, the light evoked responses after reinjection, and the lack of response in control experiments (a naïve monkey, tissue growth, blue light) support our finding that optical stimulation of neural tissue expressing Jaws increased ECoG power, despite Jaws being an inhibitory opsin. This increase could be due to disinhibition of neurons in lower cortical layers following inhibition of upper cortical layers—we reason the disinhibition is reflected in the ECoG signal through apical dendrites from the lower layers.

Given the increase of ECoG power when inhibition was applied in vivo, we examined the potential underlying mechanism by performing a simulation experiment, investigating the effect of stimulation across different cortical depths. We used VERTEX55, a simulation tool based on detailed cortical neuronal data56 used for modeling and simulating large-scale networks of neurons, which were recently updated to support optogenetic stimulations57. We found that pan-neuronal stimulation of Jaws-expressing neurons led to decreased spiking in upper layers (L2/3 and L4) and increased spiking in layer 5 (L5; Supplementary Fig. 5a, b). Similar changes are observed in local field potential (LFP) spectrograms from different cortical layers (Supplementary Fig. 5c). The observation of rebound effect in simulation also corroborates in vivo laser stimulation data (e.g., Fig. 5f), where neural responses can persist to some degree after stimulation terminates. These simulation results further confirm our hypothesis that inhibition of upper cortical layers generated disinhibition of neurons in lower cortical layers.

Stimulation during behavior
To demonstrate our platform’s applicability for behavioral neuroscience experiments, we trained the monkeys to perform a center-out reach task using their right hand (Fig. 7a) collecting data over multiple sessions (e.g., Supplementary Fig. 6). To begin, the monkey held his finger at a start target in the center of a screen, and then the end target displayed on the screen randomly in four locations: right, up, left, and down. We applied optical stimulation for 900 ms with all LEDs of our red 4 × 4 array (~12 mW/mm2) simultaneously for a randomly selected 50% of the trials with the expectation that optogenetic inhibition would impede reach. The onset of the stimulation aligned with the appearance of the end target. After a random delay, an audial “go-tone” would play, signaling the monkey to reach for the end target. Monkeys typically completed the reach before the end of stimulation.

Optogenetic inhibition led to significantly longer reach times in both monkeys (H: p = 0.04, L: p = 0.009; Fig. 7c, f); however, trajectories of the reaches during stimulated and non-stimulated conditions do not look qualitatively different (Fig. 7b, e). To better investigate these delays, we analyzed reach times for each movement direction individually (Fig. 7c, f). We found direction-specific effects in both animals. In Monkey L, reaches in the down and left directions were significantly impacted by stimulation (down p = 0.0001, left p = 0.03, up p = 0.33, right p = 1.0) (Fig. 7f). In Monkey H, significant delays were observed in the downward direction as well (down p = 0.03, left p = 0.23, up p = 0.99, right p = 0.13) (Fig. 7c). Additional analyses of path length were consistent with these findings (H all directions p = 0.40, down p = 0.04, left p = 0.35, up p = 0.08, right p = 0.32; L all directions p = 4.2e−6, down p = 1.1e−11, left p = 3.1e−5, up p = 0.45, right p = 0.71) (Fig. 7d, g).

We analyzed the neural activity recorded during reaches with and without optogenetic stimulation to identify the change in neural activity underlying the reach disruption (see Methods for details on the neural data analysis; data adapted from ref. 58). We plotted heatmaps of theta-band activity (4–10 Hz) during rest and during the planning phase of the task just before go-tone (Fig. 8a, b). The theta band is known to be reflective of behaviorally relevant cortical activity. We found that area 7 exhibits increased activity during the planning phase.

Next, we selected example electrodes in opsin expressing and deficient regions of area 7 and analyzed the signal during the planning period of the task with and without stimulation (Fig. 8c–e). To assess the changes in local activity of the selected electrodes, we analyzed high-gamma band activity. For both animals, both electrodes exhibited similar increases in baseline-normalized high-gamma-band activity during the task in the absence of stimulation. For each monkey, both electrodes had statistically significant increases in activity when stimulated (H expressing: p = 8.9e−29 deficient: p = 1.0e−5; L: expressing: p = 2.5e−114; deficient: p = 8.9e−13, Fig. 8f, g). Additionally, for both monkeys we found that the stimulation-evoked activity of the electrode over the opsin expressing area was more pronounced than the electrode over the opsin deficient area to a statistically significant degree (Monkey H: p = 2.8e−15; Monkey L: p = 8.9e−104), which was not the case in the absence of stimulation (Monkey H: p = 0.40; Monkey L: p = 0.08; Fig. 8f, g). These results support our finding that optical stimulation of neural tissue expressing Jaws increased ECoG power both during behavior and at rest (Fig. 6).
