## Methods

Multi-modal artificial dura (MMAD)
We embedded a multi-modal artificial dura (ECoG array), similar to past work41, into a traditional artificial dura (Fig. 1b). Briefly, the MMAD consisted of four conductive layers sandwiched between five transparent layers of medical-grade copolymer, where the conductive layers were aligned with each other to maximize optical access. Conductive layers were composed of platinum particles dispersed in a matrix within the polymer for mechanical flexibility. This design eliminated the need for attached printed circuit boards (PCBs), enabling long-term implantation without the challenges of protecting PCBs from moisture and fluids within the chamber. The MMAD was developed in close collaboration with Ripple Neuro (Salt Lake City, UT, USA), which manufactured the arrays. The company’s sales team may be contacted for ordering details.

A traditional artificial dura is typically described as “top-hat” shaped: a single silicone piece is composed of a cylindrical wall with an optical window at the lower end and a flange extending under the native dura to reduce regrowth of the native dura (Fig. 1b)24–26. Here, we embedded the MMAD into the artificial dura with a simple molding process40,42. The molded device is an artificial dura (skirt Ø: 31.2 mm; skirt thickness: 0.4 mm; wall outer Ø: 21.0 mm; wall inner Ø: 18.6 mm; height: 11.9 mm) with a fully embedded MMAD to allow for electrical recording and stimulation from 32 electrodes (Fig. 1b).

We designed the entire MMAD, including the cables, as a corrosion-resistant single piece. We housed the cables of the MMAD in the chamber between experiments, and during experiments, we attached the cables to the electrophysiological recording and stimulation hardware.

Chamber
The chamber is a cylinder (internal Ø 23 mm), 3D-printed and milled from titanium (Ti-6Al-4V, Hybex Innovations, Anjou, Quebec, Canada), which provides a sturdy base for experimental equipment and protect the brain when the monkey is freely moving between experiments, similar to previous work26. To design the chamber to fit the skull of each monkey, we developed a software pipeline (MATLAB, MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA; Solidworks, Waltham, MA, USA) to extract the skull curvature from an MRI file and then used the curvature to design a chamber with a unique skull-fitting skirt (Fig. 1a, c; Supplementary Fig. 7)39,40. We included an intra-cranial rim under the skirt (Supplementary Fig. 7) to aid in positioning the chamber on the skull during surgery and to reduce bone growth around the wall of the craniotomy, and included 12 holes in the skirt (Supplementary Fig. 7) for titanium screws (Crist Instrument Company, Hagerstown, MD, USA). We incorporated concentric tracks within the chamber to store the MMAD cables between experiments (Fig. 1b–d). We threaded the chamber with a high thread pitch (M38 × 1.5) to allow either affixation of experimental equipment or a cap to close the chamber between experiments (Fig. 1c; Supplementary Fig. 7).

Cap
We designed a cap (stainless steel 304, machined by Hybex Innovations) to close off the chamber between experiments. We applied polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) tape to the threads before each closure to prevent binding of the threads. We used a set screw (not shown) (HSS11400187HD, #4-40 × 3/16) to fasten the cap shut against the top rim of the chamber.

Electrophysiology hardware
Our electrophysiology setup included a ring, a clamp connector tray, and PCB clamp connectors (Fig. 1e, f). To prepare our platform for recording and stimulation, we screwed the ring onto the chamber and secured the clamp connector tray onto the ring with 2-4 screws (M2.5 × 6). The ring was machined from stainless steel (304; Hybex Innovations) and the clamp connector tray was 3D printed with titanium (TI-64; i.materialise, Leuven, Belgium).

The ring had 32 screw holes (M2.5) around its rim to offer optimal flexibility in the orientation of attachments. The upper face of the ring included a slight recess just above the threads for additional hardware to be easily aligned with the ring for fastening.

The bottom of the clamp connector tray included an intra-ring rim around the window to fit into the recess of the ring. The base of the tray included a right-angled outer rim for grounding electronics as well as four elevated screw holes (M2.5 or 4–40 thread) designed for optical stimulation equipment to be secured to the tray. We designed the tray to be compatible with both this work’s LED-based optical stimulation setup and our lab’s previously described fiber optic-based setup26. We designed the arms of the tray to be low weight and provide support for the MMAD cables as they extended from the artificial dura walls at 45°. The distal end of the tray arm was approximately 9.5 cm away from the cranial window.

The arms of the tray supported PCB clamp connectors (Fig. 1e, f; Ripple Neuro) held in place by rubber bands (not shown), which secured the MMAD cables approximately 4.5 cm away from the brain and provided an electrical connection between the cables and commercial neurophysiology equipment (Grapevine Nomad, Ripple Neuro). Two of these setups may be simultaneously deployed bilaterally, although this work is exclusive to the left hemisphere.

Optical stimulation hardware
To optically stimulate across large cortical areas (~1 cm2), we incorporated either a 4 × 4 or a 3 × 5 LED array (Fig. 2). The full 4 × 4 array was used for stimulation during reaches. To prevent LED arrays from moving when in use, we designed a system involving a rod, tube, coverslip, and stimulation holder (Fig. 1g). We custom designed and 3D printed the rod, tube, and stimulation holder in-house with FDM PLA (M2 rev G, MakerGear LLC, Beachwood, OH, USA). We glued (Better Ultimate Adhesive, slow dry, Cemedine Co. Ltd., Shinagawa City, Tokyo, Japan) the coverslip (Ø 16 mm, ORSAtec, Bobingen, Germany) to one end of the tube. The base, which we affixed to the clamp connector tray, secured the coverslip against the top side of the MMAD and a set screw (HSS11400187HD, #4–40 × 3/16) secured the rod inside the tube. The rod positioned the LED array over the brain and above the coverslip. Our setup created an air gap between the LEDs and the coverslip, which protected the brain from conductive heating. Four screws in the base secure the tube in place.

The LED array consisted of a circular custom rigid printed circuit board (PCB; Ø 15.5 mm; OSH Park, Portland, OR, USA). The LEDs (L1C1-RED1 or L1C1-BLU1, Lumileds, Schipol, Netherlands) of the 3 × 5 array were individually addressable, while the 4 × 4 array was wired to drive four individually addressable columns of LEDs. Both PCB versions included an internal copper plane for heat dissipation. We soldered the LEDs on one side of the PCB and a connector (501331-0807, Molex Inc., Lisle, IL, USA) on the other side. We drove the LEDs with a custom external PCB (OSH Park) connected to the LED array by a cable assembly (151330806, Molex Inc.). The external PCB consisted of voltage-controlled current sources. Each driving circuit consisted of a high output current op amp (TLE2301, Texas Instruments, Dallas, TX, USA) with a capacitor between the compensation network terminals and a resistor (15 Ω, 5 W, SMW515RJT, TE Connectivity, Schaffhausen, Switzerland), where the resistor value controls the ratio of input voltage to output current. The input voltage is provided by our neurophysiology system’s analog voltage output (Ripple Neuro) and is prevented from floating high (e.g., when the neurophysiology system is turned off) by a pull-down resistor (10 kΩ). We powered our PCBs with two in-series batteries (9 V Li-ion rechargeable, Keenstone, Industry, CA, USA) to reduce line noise in our electrophysiological recordings. We depict our circuit and arrays in Fig. 2 and Supplementary Fig. 1.

We also designed our clamp connector tray to be compatible with our previous laser stimulation setup30, and its slightly modified version is briefly described here. Our setup was composed of a base similar to the base for the LED array setup, and a stimulation ring, both FDM 3D-printed in-house with black PLA. The base was screwed to the clamp connector tray. The stimulation ring guided telescoping cannulas (HTX-13R, HTX-16T, and HTX-18T, Component Supply Co., Sparta, TN, USA) to different stimulation locations, and optical fibers were slid through the cannulas. We coupled lasers (520 nm or 638 nm, LDFLS_520_520_638_638, Doric Lenses, Quebec, Canada) to the optical fibers.

Animals
We recruited two healthy, socially housed male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta; Monkey H: 9 y, 13 kg; Monkey L: 9 y, 11 kg) for this study. Water was available ad libitum and standard food rations were provided after experimental sessions. All animal care and experiments were approved by the University of Washington’s Office of Animal Welfare, the University of Washington’s Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee, and the Washington National Primate Research Center.

Surgical procedures
We performed surgical procedures on both monkeys similar to procedures in other work26. We sedated the monkey and shaved its head before anesthetizing and head-fixing him in a stereotactic frame. The respiratory rate, heart rate, and body temperature of the monkey were monitored throughout the procedure. We created an incision several cm long to the left of the head’s midline and used elevators to peel back the skin, musculature, and muscle fascia. We confirmed the location of the center of the craniotomy with stereotactic coordinates. Using a Ø 25-mm trephine, we created the craniotomy. Then we resected the dura by lifting the dura with a curved needle and trimming with ophthalmic scissors, revealing the posterior parietal cortex. After test-fitting the titanium chamber to the skull, we placed a flat transparent silicone artificial dura on the brain to keep the brain moist.

With the craniotomy complete, we performed convection-enhanced delivery (CED) of Jaws (rAAV8/hSyn-Jaws-KGC-GFP-ER2, 5.4 × 1012 genome copies per milliliter (gc/mL), University of North Carolina Vector Core), a red-shifted inhibitory viral vector52. Prior to surgery, we had manufactured a 1-mm stepped-tip silica cannula (inner cannula: inner Ø 320 µm, outer Ø 435 µm; outer cannula: inner Ø 450 µm, outer Ø 673 µm; Polymicro Technologies, Phoenix, AZ, USA) for CED similar to our previous work26,51 by applying cyanoacrylate (superglue) to the inner cannula, sliding the outer cannula over the inner cannula, and using a razor blade to trim the inner cannula extending from one side of the outer cannula to make a 1-mm stepped-tip. We removed the artificial dura from the brain, punched a hole through the artificial dura to be used for our injection, laid the artificial dura back on the brain to keep the brain moist, and then inserted the cannula tip through the hole approximately 2 mm into the cortex (Fig. 3a, left) and began the infusion protocol using convection-enhanced delivery similar to previous work26. We infused up to 50 µL at each of several locations across the cortex. Once complete, we placed a new artificial dura on the brain.

Unlike previous work where live-MRI was performed during infusions26,50, we performed the infusions without live-MRI. This allowed CED to be performed in the surgery suite, while we were able to visually inspect the location of the infusion for any reflux. It also eliminates the need for MRI-compatible syringe pumps or complicated fluid line setups—the syringe and cannula were attached directly to the pump, and a stereotactic arm was used for cannula insertion during CED.

Following CED, we used a piezo-drill (5120063AS animal science package, insert tips IM1-AL and IM1S, Piezosurgery Inc., Columbus, OH) to drill screw holes and used titanium tap screws (Crist Instrument Company) to secure the chamber to the skull. We removed the artificial dura and placed the MMAD on the brain and housed the cables in the slots of the chamber (Fig. 1d). Finally, we applied PTFE tape to the threads, closed the cap, secured the set screw, and applied bone wax to the set screw. Having secured and closed the chamber, we closed the wound using standard surgical techniques.

We had implanted a titanium headpost (Crist Instrument Company) on each monkey prior to this study39.

Chamber cleaning and hardware assembly
We developed a process of cleaning the chamber at least three times each week, starting one week after the surgery. We briefly describe the processes here. After head-fixing the monkey, we cleaned the cap, chamber margin, surrounding scalp and outside of the ear. Once clean, we removed the cap and cleaned the margin. We used sterile cotton-tipped applicators dipped in saline to clean the threads and the rim of the chamber. To clean the inside of the chamber, we used a sterile syringe and blunt-tipped needle to irrigate warm sterile saline on and in the MMAD, its cables, and the storage area for the cables.

To prepare for electrophysiological recording, we screwed a sterile ring onto the chamber and screwed a sterile clamp connector tray to the ring with sterile screws. Then we removed the cables from the chamber and placed them into the clamp connectors, and rubber banded the clamp connectors to the clamp connector tray arms.

To prepare for optical stimulation, we attached the stimulation holder for either the LED array or the lasers. In the case of laser stimulation, we slid the stimulation ring down around the stimulation holder and inserted the fiber optic cable through the cannula and placed the cannula on top of the brain through the stimulation ring. In the case of LED stimulation, we assembled the LED array, rod, and tube with coverslip, and secured them together with a set screw. Then we lowered the assembly down through the stimulation holder and into the MMAD, and secured the tube into place with set screws. Black foil was wrapped around the stimulation equipment to prevent the monkey from seeing any lighting changes in the experimental rig due to stimulation.

When the experiment was complete, we removed the stimulation and recording equipment, cleaned the MMAD, and used sterile forceps to return the cables back into the chamber. Then we cleaned the chamber using sterile saline irrigation and applied an antibiotic to the center of the MMAD. To avoid building antibiotic resistance, we rotated through polymyxin B sulfate, gentamicin, and amikacin sulfate antibiotics, applying one for 4-5 weeks and then switching to the next. To prevent the cap from binding to the chamber between cleanings, we wrapped a strip of sterile PTFE around a portion of the threads. Then we screwed on a sterile cap and a set screw.

Epifluorescence imaging
We performed epifluorescence imaging of green fluorescence protein (GFP) by using a blue light for the excitation wavelength of GFP (NIGHTSEA stereo microscope fluorescence adapter, SFA-RB royal blue, Electron Microscopy Sciences, Hatfield, PA) in combination with a DSLR camera (Nikon D5300, Minato City, Tokyo, Japan) and a lens based on the emission wavelength of the GFP (Nikon DX AF-S NIKKOR 35mm 1:1.8G, SWM Aspherical ∞-0.3m/0.98ft Ø 52) for imaging. We illuminated the brain from multiple angles to fully cover the optical window. The camera was fixed throughout the illumination process, which eased stitching the photos together with image editing software.

Expression coverage was measured by outlining the extent of expression in the stitched epifluorescent image manually, counting the number of pixels within the outlined areas, and converting to mm2 based on known distances in the image, i.e., the distance between electrodes.

Behavioral task
Our center-out reach task (Fig. 7a) was controlled by custom software in MATLAB using Psychophysics Toolbox version 3123–125, similar to previous work126. A reflective sticker, placed on the middle finger of the monkey’s right hand, contralateral to the implant, was tracked by a motion capture system (Motive, OptiTrack, NaturalPoint Inc., Corvallis, OR, USA). These tracking data were processed in real-time by MATLAB. The monkey was rewarded for successful trials with juice (5-RLD-D1 D.A.R.I.S., Crist Instrument Company). The monkey was head-fixed and seated in a monkey chair inside a dark experimental rig. The visual and audio stimuli were provided by a monitor with built-in speakers within reaching distance of the monkey.

Monkeys performed several hundred trials each session (Monkey H: mean trials per session: 557.7, standard deviation: 217.6; Monkey L: mean trials per session: 715.7, standard deviation: 266.0). For Monkey H, there were 4522 analyzed reach trials split over 8 sessions, while for Monkey L there were 11,101 trials split over 13 sessions.

Behavioral analysis
We analyzed reaches from the behavioral trials. All successful trials from all sessions were labeled with reach direction (right, down, left, or up) and stimulation condition (stimulation or no stimulation). Data groups were compared statistically by Mann–Whitney U test of the distribution of reach times. Our experimental design focused on examining how stimulation would affect behavioral metrics, including reach time, path length and direction, which we carefully recorded. For these hypotheses, we did not adjust p-values as the nature of our analysis was not exploratory.

We tracked the reach path and reach time and analyzed movement in three-dimensional space for both stimulation and control (no stimulation) conditions. We measured the time between the go-tone and the finger’s entry into the end target, and we call this time the “reach time”.

Behavioral data preprocessing
All reach trials were aggregated over all dates and conditions for each monkeys individually. Trials were excluded from analysis if the reach was unsuccessful or if the trail was a warm up trial as judged from a wait time before the go-tone <0.3 s, or a circle size >50 pixels radius (approx. 25 mm diameter).

The neural data were screened to remove malfunctioning electrodes by measuring the impedance of the electrodes and by visual inspection of the voltage traces. Additionally, the standard deviation of the raw neural signal was computed for each trial, and if the z-score of the standard deviation was >6, the trial was excluded.

Neural data analysis
Neural activity was recorded during behavior and stimulation (1 kHz sampling frequency, Grapevine Nomad, Ripple Neuro). All neural data analyses were conducted separately for the two monkeys. High impedance electrodes were excluded from analyses.

The process involved segregating all trials into stimulation and non-stimulation trials. Each trial was then split into three epochs: before stimulation, during stimulation (or during when the stimulation would have occurred), and after stimulation. We analyzed 500 ms of local field potential (LFP) activity immediately preceding the onset of stimulation (“before stimulation”). The “during stimulation” period encompassed the 900 ms of LFP recorded during stimulation, and the “after stimulation” period covered the 900 ms following the end of stimulation. Artifact removal was applied to each epoch (see “Photo-Induced Artifact Removal” section below).

After removing photo-induced artifact, we quantified the effect of stimulation by analyzing the time-frequency content of the data. Multitaper spectrograms of ECoG data from each trial were calculated with 50-ms non-overlapping windows, five tapers and a 128-sample length Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) between 1 and 200 Hz. The values of each bin are normalized by the 500-ms pre-stimulation activity. The 50 ms immediately following the start and termination of stimulation are excluded from analysis to avoid including any residual artifact in the signal at these times.

To quantify the changes due to stimulation, we calculated the average values of the spectrogram per frequency bin. Spectrograms were normalized to the 500 ms preceding stimulation and the resulting values were used to determine if statistically significant changes were induced before, during, and after stimulation using the Mann–Whitney U test. For control experiments, the data processing matched the stimulated condition, although the stimulation did not occur.

Photo-induced artifact removal
To isolate photo-induced artifacts from the electrocorticography acquired during simultaneous optical stimulation in vivo, we generated a dataset of these artifacts, absent any neural signals, by optically stimulating an electrode array submerged in a saline bath. We modeled the photo-induced artifact using these saline data, fit the model to the in vivo ECoG, and removed the estimated photo-induced artifact. The procedure involved the following steps (Supplementary Fig. 8):

1. The time surrounding each stimulation in the saline data was isolated, from 100 ms before the onset of stimulation to one second after the end of stimulation. Each of the 32 channels were stacked with their 100 corresponding stimulation pulses to form a matrix (32 × 100 × length of time).

2. The matrix was split along the time axis into three matrices corresponding to before stimulation, during stimulation, and after stimulation.

3. The saline data at the time of stimulation onset and offset (data point time=0 for matrices “during stimulation” and “after stimulation,” respectively) were set to 0 mV and the whole traces were shifted accordingly.

4. Photo-induced artifact was modeled from these data using principal component analysis (PCA) conducted separately on the “during stimulation” and “after stimulation” matrices, with the top three components extracted from each.

This model was subsequently employed to eliminate the artifact from the in vivo data as follows:

5. The in vivo data were isolated and stacked in the same way as the saline data, such that a data matrix (channels × pulses × length of time), with identical time length, was formed.

6. The matrix was split along the time axis into three matrices corresponding to before stimulation, during stimulation, and after stimulation.

7. The ECoG data at the time of stimulation onset and offset (data point time=0 for matrices “during stimulation” and “after stimulation”) were set to 0 mV and the whole traces were shifted accordingly.

8. The ECoG data from the “during stimulation” and “after stimulation” matrices were projected onto the corresponding models derived from saline, and the estimated photo-induced artifact was regressed out of the NHP data using linear regression.

9. The three matrices were rejoined along the time axis, adding an offset to the later matrices such that the average LFP value of the last 50 ms of the preceding matrix and the first 50 ms of the later matrix had the same average value.

This procedure enabled the separation of the photo-induced artifact from neural activity, and retaining the neural activity in the recorded signal (Fig. 4; Supplementary Fig. 8), as confirmed by controls (Fig. 4).

Simulation
We simulated large-scale neural spiking activity and LFPs across cortical layers using the extended VERTEX model, which allows for optogenetic stimulation and neural activity recording57. The tissue model was 1.5 × 1.5 × 2.6 mm deep with LFP recording sites arranged in a 3 × 3 × 6 grid, and a 200 µm optical fiber placed orthogonally at the center of the cortical surface (Supplementary Fig. 9). We used the VERTEX Jaws opsin model, which hyperpolarizes neuronal membrane currents when optically evoked. Optogenetic inhibition was modeled with a train of optical pulses matching our experimental conditions (594 nm wavelength, 10 pulses, 900 ms on/2900 ms off). To examine local firing rates around the optic fiber, Supplementary Fig. 5a, b show neuron firing rates along the z-axis within a 400 µm cylinder around the optical fiber. Supplementary Fig. 5c shows the time-frequency spectrogram of the LFP recording sites centered in each layer.

### Reviewer 3

The manuscript presents a comprehensive account of a large-scale optogenetic neurophysiology platform designed for non-
human primates (NHP) and illustrates its application in a behavioral study. While the organization and clarity of the
manuscript are commendable, I have considerable reservations about the novelty and scientific importance of this work,
particularly in relation to its potential publication in Nature Communications.
One of the main challenges facing optogenetics in primate research is the effective outcome of behavioral manipulation,
especially regarding motor actions. In its current form, the study utilizing the assembled platform does not significantly
advance this field. Although it shows some impact on reaching behaviors, I question the practicality of the platform as
presented, regardless of its apparent complexity.
Furthermore, if the objective is to utilize this device for exploring the neural mechanisms behind specific cognitive functions
or understanding network dynamics, the existing design offers no distinct advantages over current technologies. The ECoG
array is limited to capturing local field potentials, and the extensive LED array suffers from inadequate spatial resolution and
substantial interference artifacts. Together, these limitations render the system less appealing.
To enhance the design, I propose the following suggestions:
1. Consider replacing the LED array with a micro-LED array to improve spatial resolution (doi.org/10.1038/s41592-021-
01238-9). This micro-LED array could be programmed for high temporal resolution, theoretically producing lower artifacts
and thereby increasing the likelihood of capturing transient changes in neural activity. Additionally, implementing an LED
array with dual wavelengths could facilitate simultaneous activation and deactivation using one device.
2. I recommend mapping the finger and arm zones prior to light stimulation. Random stimulation tends to be less effective in
eliciting behavioral responses. I encourage the authors to adopt a different strategy: record neural activity during reaching
tasks across a broad cortical area, and subsequently program the micro-LED array to illuminate the brain in alignment with
the recorded activation patterns. Given that these patterns will vary in both space and time, mastering the programming of
the LED array is crucial.
Specific concerns include:
1. I find the rationale behind the unexpected increase in ECoG signals unconvincing. A straightforward verification could be
conducted through single-unit recordings.
2. Although the authors conducted control experiments to indicate that responses were largely optogenetically induced, they
were unable to completely eliminate the thermal effects. Therefore, an additional control trial involving non-expressing
monkeys (or the same monkey before viral injection) remains necessary. While I acknowledge the associated challenges,
the experiment, as it stands, lacks thoroughness.

### Reviewer 4

Griggs and colleagues present an integrated optogenetic and electrocorticography (ECoG) platform designed for use in
macaques. This is an impressive technical achievement, combining optogenetic modulation with large-scale neural
recordings. While similar techniques have been proposed individually or with more complex approaches, this tool seems
relatively straightforward to implement in a lab with enough technical expertise. I highly commend the authors for developing
and utilizing such an innovative piece of technology. I’m convinced many will be interested in these tools.
However, I find myself less convinced by the neuroscientific aspects of the manuscript. As the authors themselves highlight,
it is puzzling to observe a net increase in LFP power following Jaws stimulation. While optogenetic stimulation with a
hyperpolarizing opsin is known to induce a mixture of inhibitory and excitatory effects at the single-unit level, population-
level effects should generally lead to net inhibition. The weak behavioral effects observed also suggest that the output of the
stimulated region might be slightly reduced, which contradicts the observed increase in LFP power. In my view, this
unexpected result warrants further explanation and exploration. Given the substantial light-induced artifacts observed in
saline (Fig. S5), I am still uncertain whether these effects are truly neuronal, despite the authors’ counter-arguments.
I was surprised that the authors averaged their results across all ECoG channels (Fig. 4 G-O; 7). Surely, in Figure 5, they
distinguish between transduced and non-transduced sectors. I recommend that they apply a similar analysis based on the
functional properties of the cortex under the electrodes. For example, by using task-induced neuronal activity (such as
reaching-related activity) from both transduced and non-transduced areas, they could define regions of interest (ROIs)
across 4 different cortical regions (transduced or not, functionally relevant or not). This would allow for a more refined
analysis of the data.
Moreover, it would be valuable to replicate these experiments using a penetrating electrode (e.g., a laminar probe) to
compare the surprising ECoG data with single- or multi-unit recordings, providing additional insight into the neuronal effects.
In summary, this is a highly interesting technical paper that somehow should be published, but I believe it should be
considered for its methodological contributions rather than its neuroscientific conclusions. As such, I am presently
unconvinced it is suitable for publication in Nature Communications. IMHO, a more thorough investigation of the neuronal
and behavioral effects (see below) is warranted, but I refrain to the editors to make that call.
Minor Comments:
1. Method Limitations: The authors highlight the advantages of their new method but should also mention its limitations. For
example, the method is limited to recording from superficial, easily accessible parts of the cortex and cannot capture data
from structures buried in sulci or from deeper cortical areas that are not accessible with the current setup. Surely, more
limitations can be listed.
2. Neuronal Data with Dura Resection: The authors mention that their MMAD allows recording for 10-14 weeks, after which
dura growth requires resection. While stability of GFP expression is clearly illustrated in Figure 3, it would be informative to
include raw neuronal traces for the same periods, along with both GFP and neuronal data after multiple dura resections
(e.g., approximately 2-3 years post-implant).
3. Figure 3C: This figure requires more explanation. It is unclear what point the authors are trying to make, and further
clarification would be helpful.
4. Figure 4: The fonts and arrowheads in this figure are barely visible. Please increase their size for better clarity.
5. Figure 4 Statistical Analysis: I suspect the statistics in Figure 4 use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. It is unusual to observe
significant changes in the pre-stimulation period. Was a correction for multiple comparisons applied? If not, this should be
done. If a correction was applied, could the authors explain the pre-stimulation differences?
6. Non-Neuronal Effects: The authors argue that the ECoG responses are “primarily” optogenetically evoked (non-thermal).
However, control experiments indicate substantial non-neuronal effects. Can the authors estimate the contributions of these
two effects (neuronal vs. non-neuronal) to the observed in vivo data?
7. Behavioral Data Statistical Analysis: Was a correction for multiple comparisons applied to the behavioral data? If not, I
suggest this be done to ensure the robustness of the results.
8. Spatially-Specific Behavioral Effects: I was surprised by the lack of consistent spatially-specific behavioral effects. How
reliable were these effects across sessions or across trial blocks within the same session? Test-retest reliability should be
shown to strengthen the findings.
9. Figure 6 Significance Indicators: The asterisks indicating significance in Figure 6 do not always match the descriptions in
the text. Please check for accuracy. Were all trials included in the analysis for this figure?
10. Figure 7: As mentioned earlier, it would be highly informative to show time-frequency plots for four different electrode
sites (transduced vs. non-transduced and task-modulated vs. non-task-modulated sites).
11. Interpretation of Reaching Behavior: The authors interpret the stimulation-induced changes in reaching behavior as
changes in motor dynamics. However, this region of the parietal cortex is involved in a variety of interrelated functions,
including but not restricted to e.g. attention, multisensory integration, and decision-making. How do the authors disentangle
these contributions from the motor changes observed in the reaching task?

exploratory analysis such as this, where we find specific time-frequency bins that are modulated

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Griggs et al. presents a cost-effective and scalable platform capable of multimodal
optogenetic and neurophysiological studies in behaving macaques positioned in a primate chair. In
contrast to other published macaque chamber-mounted systems, the key advances of this platform
include its scalability, the integration of LFP/ECoG capabilities into the artificial dura (the MMAD), and its
ability to perform patterned optogenetic stimulation. The authors demonstrate the system’s
functionality by showcasing its capability to monitor epifluorescence (optogenetic expression) over
several months, as well as its ability to modulate LPFs and reaching behavior through optogenetic
stimulation. I commend the authors for acknowledging that the clear view of the brain through the
artificial dura typically lasts only a couple of months, after which a tissue removal procedure is required
to regain visual access for further studies. While this limitation, along with others (e.g., risk of infection,
optogenetic light artifacts in neurophysiological signals, and the focus on surface-level recordings),
constrains its ability to fully reveal the circuitry underlying behavior, the utilization of this platform can
set the stage for significant advancements in primate cognitive neuroscience.
We thank the Reviewer for their enthusiasm for our paper and for their constructive feedback,
below we have provided responses to their comments.
Major Comments

epifluorescence, since only the collection but not quantitation was described in the Star Methods; (b)
consistency of the optical window, since alignment procedures for the FOV, blood vessel changes across
days and weeks (e.g. Figure 3 top row) were not discussed; (c) LFP signals, in Figure 4 it is unclear as to
the sample size of the LFP data (e.g. number of trials), let alone whether it was collected across multiple
days or weeks); (d) behavioral measures, how consistence were the effects of optogenetic stimulation on
behavior across days.
In response to your comments regarding epifluorescence, window transparency, and behavioral
reproducibility over time, we have incorporated additional data and revisions to address these
points:
We have added new data showing changes in the optical window over several weeks (Supp. Fig.
3). Unlike some other recording and stimulation platforms, ours enables researchers to monitor
and adapt to cortical changes as they arise. While tracking blood vessel changes was not the
primary aim of this study, our platform is well-suited for such investigations. Notably, it is
compatible with optical coherence tomography angiography – a technique we have previously
demonstrated for studying vasculature. We have updated the Discussion (paragraph 3) to reflect
this.
As suggested, we now include light-evoked responses across time, which demonstrate consistent
effects over repeated sessions (Fig. 6e). In addition, we have added sample size details to Fig. 5
(formerly Fig. 4), per your request.
We have also included new data on optogenetically-evoked behavioral responses recorded across
multiple days (Supp. Fig. 6).
Finally, in response to your note about epifluorescence quantification, we have added the

immediately following stimulation onset and offset can be recovered to a degree, we did not

The manuscript presents a comprehensive account of a large-scale optogenetic neurophysiology
platform designed for non-human primates (NHP) and illustrates its application in a behavioral study.
While the organization and clarity of the manuscript are commendable, I have considerable reservations
about the novelty and scientific importance of this work, particularly in relation to its potential
publication in Nature Communications.
One of the main challenges facing optogenetics in primate research is the effective outcome of
behavioral manipulation, especially regarding motor actions. In its current form, the study utilizing the
assembled platform does not significantly advance this field. Although it shows some impact on reaching
behaviors, I question the practicality of the platform as presented, regardless of its apparent complexity.
Furthermore, if the objective is to utilize this device for exploring the neural mechanisms behind specific
cognitive functions or understanding network dynamics, the existing design offers no distinct advantages
advantages
over current technologies. The ECoG array is limited to capturing local field potentials, and the extensive
LED array suffers from inadequate spatial resolution and substantial interference artifacts. Together,
these limitations render the system less appealing.
We thank the Reviewer for their comments and constructive feedback. We have added
clarifications in response to your points, summarized below:
1. Large-scale, stable optical and electrophysiological access: Our platform provides stable optical
access to approximately 2 cm² of cortex, with electrode coverage over 1 cm². This is a distinct
advantage over many current technologies. Existing approaches often lack long-term, large-scale
access, limiting the ability to both monitor and modulate brain activity over wide networks. As
discussed in Introduction paragraph 2, such access is essential for studying brain function and
dysfunction, and for developing therapies for neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders.
2. Importance and potential of ECoG: We emphasize ECoG’s translational relevance, long-term
signal stability, and its value in studying network dynamics. While the current version of our
MMAD does not record action potentials from the cortical surface, we expect future iterations
will be able to do so—as demonstrated by us and others. We now clarify this point in Discussion
paragraph 2 and provide relevant citations.
3. Optogenetic modulation and system accessibility: Our current LED array demonstrates that
optogenetic stimulation at this resolution can influence behavior. While we are also pursuing
higher-resolution LED arrays in separate efforts, this work focuses on developing an accessible,
easy-to-build system that other non-human primate (NHP) researchers can readily adopt. A key
challenge in neuroscience today is that many advanced tools remain confined to the labs that
developed them. In contrast, we designed our system to be widely adoptable, which we view as a
strength—especially given the relatively small size of the NHP research community. As noted,
laser-based stimulation remains an option in our platform for high-resolution, targeted
applications, and we now cite a high-resolution LED solution (as the Reviewer suggested) that
users may integrate if desired.
4. Photo-induced artifact removal: We recognized and addressed photo-induced artifacts in ECoG
signals by developing an effective artifact removal method. A brief description is now included in
the Results section (“Photo-induced artifact removal”), with a detailed explanation provided in
the Methods section (“Photo-induced artifact removal”).
To enhance the design, I propose the following suggestions:
1. Consider replacing the LED array with a micro-LED array to improve spatial resolution
(doi.org/10.1038/s41592-021-01238-9). This micro-LED array could be programmed for high temporal
resolution, theoretically producing lower artifacts and thereby increasing the likelihood of capturing
transient changes in neural activity. Additionally, implementing an LED array with dual wavelengths could
facilitate simultaneous activation and deactivation using one device.
We provide further clarification below:
1. High temporal resolution of LED array: Our LED array and driving circuitry support sub-
millisecond temporal resolution. We have updated “Hardware,” paragraph 4, to emphasize this
point. Additionally, we have included new data (Supp. Vid. 1) to demonstrate the array’s ability
to support stimulation with spatiotemporal complexity and dynamic control of optical power.
2. Artifact considerations with long stimulation: While we recognize that shorter stimulation
durations reduce photo-artifact amplitude, longer durations were intentionally used in this study
to investigate reach behaviors under continuous stimulation. Importantly, we have developed an
effective artifact rejection method (see “Photo-induced artifact removal” in Results and
Methods), allowing us to analyze neural activity during stimulation, as shown throughout the
manuscript (e.g., Fig. 8).
3. Support for multiple wavelengths: Our LED array is designed with flexibility in mind—LEDs of
different colors but with a consistent footprint to ours are commercially available and allow for
easy customization of multi-color arrays. We have clarified this in Discussion paragraph 3, noting
that our design can support step-function opsins and, indeed, two wavelengths were tested in
this study.
4. Accessibility vs. complexity in array design: While we appreciate the Reviewer highlighting the
potential of advanced micro-LED technologies, including those cited, our focus is on developing
an optogenetic platform that is accessible, reproducible, and feasible for labs with modest
technical resources. This goal is central to our manuscript, as reflected in the title and overall
approach.
2. I recommend mapping the finger and arm zones prior to light stimulation. Random stimulation tends
to be less effective in eliciting behavioral responses. I encourage the authors to adopt a different
strategy: record neural activity during reaching tasks across a broad cortical area, and subsequently
program the micro-LED array to illuminate the brain in alignment with the recorded activation patterns.
Given that these patterns will vary in both space and time, mastering the programming of the LED array
is crucial.
The primary goal of this paper is to introduce a novel platform that enables simultaneous
electrophysiological recording and optogenetic stimulation across large cortical areas. Based on
feedback throughout the review process, we have further revised the manuscript to emphasize
the various components and capabilities of the technology itself.
With regard to the behavioral effects, our intent is to demonstrate the feasibility of using this
platform to induce measurable behavioral changes through optogenetic stimulation—an
achievement that has been particularly challenging, as noted in the literature. As the Reviewer
suggests, more sophisticated experiments such as patterned or closed-loop stimulation represent
exciting directions for future work, and our platform is well-suited to support such studies.
We also appreciate your comment on the importance of understanding activation patterns. To
address this, we have added a heatmap in Fig. 8 showing behaviorally relevant neural activity,
which reveals preparatory signals in the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), consistent with our
expectations. This activity spans a broad region of the network, although it is not localized to
musculoskeletal-specific areas such as arm zones in the motor cortex. As shown in Fig. 8b, the
majority of electrodes cover areas significantly modulated by reaching behavior. We speculate
that finger and arm representations may be less distinct in the PPC compared to primary motor
and premotor regions, which are more directly involved in motor control.
To clarify our stimulation protocol is not random: we employed two types of stimulation in this
study. The first is open-loop stimulation, which is delivered independently of behavior or neural
activity and is used to broadly assess stimulation effects on cortical activity. The second
is behaviorally-informed stimulation, triggered after the monkey acquires the start target, to
examine potential behavioral correlates of stimulation. This design aligns with established
approaches in behavioral neuroscience.
Although we did not implement closed-loop stimulation in this study, the hardware and software
used (Ripple Neuro) are fully compatible with such applications. Our goal in this paper is to
introduce and validate the capabilities of the platform, laying the groundwork for more
advanced experiments in future research.
Finally, we emphasize that our LED array and driving circuitry are capable of sub-millisecond
temporal resolution. We have updated the “Hardware” section (paragraph 4) to make this clear
and added new demonstration data (Supp. Vid. 1) showing the system’s capacity for complex
spatiotemporal stimulation with adjustable optical power.
Specific concerns include:
1. I find the rationale behind the unexpected increase in ECoG signals unconvincing. A straightforward
verification could be conducted through single-unit recordings.
We recognize that the observed increase in ECoG signal was unexpected, and in response, we
have conducted extensive control experiments, added a simulation study, and substantially
expanded our discussion of this finding, as also suggested by other Reviewers. These efforts have
significantly strengthened our manuscript in several key ways:
1. We introduced a novel spiking-based simulation component to investigate the mechanisms
underlying the increase in ECoG power. The results of this simulation are consistent with our in
vivo findings and provide further validation of the phenomenon. (See Results section
“Stimulation at rest,” paragraph 5; Supp. Fig. 5; Methods section “Simulation”; and Discussion,
paragraphs 9 and 10.)
2. In addition to the new data, we have incorporated relevant literature to contextualize and
support our findings. In particular, we reference our previous work, where we simultaneously
recorded from multiple cortical depths while stimulating and recording from the brain surface
using ECoG electrodes [11], [12]. Those results align well with the present findings and further
support the observed increase in ECoG activity.
Taken together, these new data, analyses, and manuscript improvements—along with the
control experiments (e.g., Fig. 5 and Fig. 6)—provide robust support for our conclusion and help
clarify the underlying mechanisms behind this unexpected result.
2. Although the authors conducted control experiments to indicate that responses were largely
optogenetically induced, they were unable to completely eliminate the thermal effects. Therefore, an
additional control trial involving non-expressing monkeys (or the same monkey before viral injection)
remains necessary. While I acknowledge the associated challenges, the experiment, as it stands,
lacks thoroughness.
To address your comment, we repeated the stimulation experiments in a naïve monkey that had
not received any optogenetic vector injection. We also added new data from another monkey
whose opsin expression had largely faded two years after viral vector infusion. These results, now
included in Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5), show comparable stimulation responses in both cases, with no
statistically significant increases in evoked activity relative to baseline. These findings in
combination with our other control experiments, support our claim that the statistically significant
stimulation-evoked activity reported throughout the paper is specific to cortical regions expressing
the opsin.

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Griggs and colleagues present an integrated optogenetic and electrocorticography (ECoG) platform
designed for use in macaques. This is an impressive technical achievement, combining optogenetic
modulation with large-scale neural recordings. While similar techniques have been proposed individually
or with more complex approaches, this tool seems relatively straightforward to implement in a lab with
enough technical expertise. I highly commend the authors for developing and utilizing such an innovative
piece of technology. I’m convinced many will be interested in these tools.
However, I find myself less convinced by the neuroscientific aspects of the manuscript. As the authors
themselves highlight, it is puzzling to observe a net increase in LFP power following Jaws stimulation.
While optogenetic stimulation with a hyperpolarizing opsin is known to induce a mixture of inhibitory
and excitatory effects at the single-unit level, population-level effects should generally lead to net
inhibition.
We thank the Reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback and have addressed their
concern through several key additions and analyses:
1. We introduced a new simulation arm to further investigate the unexpected increase in ECoG
power. The results of this simulation are consistent with our in vivo findings and are presented in
the final paragraph of the “Stimulation at rest” section, Supp. Fig. 5, and the updated Discussion
(paragraphs 9 and 10).
2. We added new data to Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) comparing stimulation responses in a naïve
monkey (with no optogenetic vector injection) and another monkey in which opsin expression
had largely faded two years post-infusion. In both cases, stimulation-evoked activity did not
significantly increase relative to baseline, supporting our claim that the statistically significant
evoked responses reported throughout the paper originate from opsin-expressing cortical
regions
3. We revised the Discussion (paragraphs 8 and 9) to provide a more detailed explanation of the
observed ECoG signal increases, supported by relevant literature. We also reference our previous
work [11], [12], in which we simultaneously recorded from multiple cortical depths while
stimulating and recording from the surface using ECoG electrodes. Those findings are consistent
with the present results and further validate the reported increase in ECoG activity.
These changes, along with our controls (e.g., Fig. 5, Fig. 6), support our finding of an increase in
ECoG signals.
The weak behavioral effects observed also suggest that the output of the stimulated region might be
slightly reduced, which contradicts the observed increase in LFP power. In my view, this unexpected
result warrants further explanation and exploration. Given the substantial light-induced artifacts
observed in saline (Fig. S5), I am still uncertain whether these effects are truly neuronal, despite the
authors’ counter-arguments.
Thank you for your interesting and thoughtful interpretations. We address these concerns in
multiple ways:
1. In our observed data, optogenetic stimulation of the posterior parietal cortex (PPC)—a
region indirectly involved in reaching—produced behavioral effects comparable to those
reported in other non-human primate (NHP) studies using electrical stimulation of motor or
premotor areas that are directly involved in reach control. As noted in the literature,
optogenetically evoked behavioral effects have been difficult to achieve. The fact that we
observed such effects from PPC stimulation, despite it not being a primary motor area,
highlights the strength of our interface: it is capable of optically modulating circuits on a
sufficiently large scale to induce measurable behavioral outcomes. We have clarified this
distinction in the Discussion, paragraphs 12 and 13.
2. Our behavioral measures demonstrate impaired reaching performance following optogenetic
stimulation. As discussed above, the observed delays are comparable to those reported with
excitatory stimulation (e.g., electrical stimulation), suggesting that in both cases, circuit
disruption is the likely underlying mechanism. Understanding the precise downstream neural
effects would require additional experiments, which are beyond the scope of the current
study.
3. We recognized that photo-induced artifacts are apparent in the ECoG signals, and therefore
we developed an effective method of removing photo-induced artifacts. We now include a
brief description of the method in the Results section (“Photo-induced artifact removal”) as
well as a more detailed description in the Methods section (“Photo-induced artifact
removal”).
4. In response to the general concern regarding our unexpected finding that activation of an
inhibitory opsin led to increased ECoG power, we have made substantial revisions to the
manuscript. These additions—including new data and improved contextual explanations—
collectively strengthen the validity of our findings:
a. We introduced a new simulation model to further investigate the observed increase in
ECoG power. The simulation results are consistent with our in vivo data (see the final
paragraph of the “Stimulation at rest” section, Supp. Fig. 5, and Discussion paragraphs 9
and 10).
b. We added data examining the relationship between opsin expression and neural
activity during reach behavior (see the final paragraph of the Results section and Fig. 8).
c. We expanded Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) to include longitudinal stimulation data.
d. We also included stimulation results from a naïve (non-expressing) animal (Fig. 6d).
This animal, along with another in which opsin expression had faded over time, showed
no significant stimulation-evoked activity relative to baseline. These data further support
our claim that significant responses were specific to opsin-expressing regions.
e. We expanded our discussion of the functional roles of areas 5 and 7 in reaching
behavior, incorporating relevant literature as suggested (see Discussion, paragraph 12).
Together with our control data (e.g., Figs. 5 and 6), these revisions provide a more
comprehensive and well-supported interpretation of the observed increase in ECoG activity.
Please note that Supp. Fig. 5 has been split into two new places: Fig. 4 and Supp. Fig. 8.
I was surprised that the authors averaged their results across all ECoG channels (Fig. 4 G-O; 7). Surely, in
Figure 5, they distinguish between transduced and non-transduced sectors. I recommend that they apply
a similar analysis based on the functional properties of the cortex under the electrodes. For example, by
using task-induced neuronal activity (such as reaching-related activity) from both transduced and non-
transduced areas, they could define regions of interest (ROIs) across 4 different cortical regions
(transduced or not, functionally relevant or not). This would allow for a more refined analysis of the
data.
In response, we have revised the manuscript to include data from individual electrodes,
separated by opsin expression status, behavioral and stimulation state and removed the previous
Fig. 7, which pooled data across conditions. We believe that the revised Figs. 5 and 6, and newly
added Fig. 8, now address the Reviewer’s concerns more effectively.
Specifically, Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) now distinguishes between electrodes located in opsin-
expressing versus non-expressing regions. In addition, we have collected and incorporated new
data comparing reach-related activity between stimulated and non-stimulated conditions, and
between opsin-expressing and non-expressing areas, as suggested by the Reviewer (Fig. 8).
As shown in Fig. 8b, ECoG signals from the majority of electrodes are modulated by reach
behavior. This is consistent with the role of the PPC, which is known to support complex
multisensory integration for goal-directed actions. Unlike the motor and somatosensory
cortices—which are more precisely subdivided by body part—the PPC integrates information
across modalities and effectors, and such broad activation is expected.
Please note that Figs. 4 and 5 have been renumbered as Figs. 5 and 6, respectively.
Moreover, it would be valuable to replicate these experiments using a penetrating electrode (e.g., a
laminar probe) to compare the surprising ECoG data with single- or multi-unit recordings, providing
additional insight into the neuronal effects.
While we agree that this is an exciting direction, it is unfortunately beyond the scope of the
current study, as our present platform design does not support simultaneous ECoG and depth
recordings during optical stimulation.
However, to further investigate the unexpected increase in ECoG power, we have added a new
optogenetic simulation model to the study. This model allows for simulated recordings of both
spikes and LFPs at multiple cortical depths during surface optical stimulation. The simulation
results are consistent with our in vivo findings (see the final paragraph of the “Stimulation at
rest” section, Supplementary Fig. 5, and Discussion paragraphs 9 and 10).
In addition, we compare our results to previous work in which we recorded simultaneously from
various cortical depths and the brain surface using ECoG during surface stimulation [11], [12].
Those findings also align well with the observations reported in this study.
In summary, this is a highly interesting technical paper that somehow should be published, but I believe
it should be considered for its methodological contributions rather than its neuroscientific conclusions.
As such, I am presently unconvinced it is suitable for publication in Nature Communications. IMHO, a
more thorough investigation of the neuronal and behavioral effects (see below) is warranted, but I
refrain to the editors to make that call.
Minor Comments:
1. Method Limitations: The authors highlight the advantages of their new method but should also
mention its limitations. For example, the method is limited to recording from superficial, easily
accessible parts of the cortex and cannot capture data from structures buried in sulci or from deeper
cortical areas that are not accessible with the current setup. Surely, more limitations can be listed.
While we do not include a formal limitations section, we have acknowledged the limitations of
our system throughout the Discussion. These include finite temporal and spatial optical access,
a restriction to 32 recording channels, the invasiveness of the chamber implantation procedure,
and other practical considerations.
2. Neuronal Data with Dura Resection: The authors mention that their MMAD allows recording for 10-14
weeks, after which dura growth requires resection. While stability of GFP expression is clearly illustrated
in Figure 3, it would be informative to include raw neuronal traces for the same periods, along with both
GFP and neuronal data after multiple dura resections (e.g., approximately 2-3 years post-implant).
In response, we have:
1. Added ECoG traces in Fig. 4.
2. Added epifluorescence data after 97 weeks in Monkey H (Fig. 6b) and before and after
reinjection in Monkey L (Fig. 6e, insets).
3. Added ECoG data of electrodes in opsin expressing and deficient regions across time (Fig. 6e).
The data include stimulation-evoked ECoG responses after initial injection, reinjection, and
dura resection. Please note that most of the sessions report statistically significant responses.
3. Figure 3C: This figure requires more explanation. It is unclear what point the authors are trying to
make, and further clarification would be helpful.
The figure has been reconfigured as a pie-graph for clarity.
4. Figure 4: The fonts and arrowheads in this figure are barely visible. Please increase their size for better
clarity.
We have enlarged Fig. 5 (formerly Fig. 4) and improved its resolution.
5. Figure 4 Statistical Analysis: I suspect the statistics in Figure 4 use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. It is
unusual to observe significant changes in the pre-stimulation period. Was a correction for multiple
comparisons applied? If not, this should be done. If a correction was applied, could the authors explain
the pre-stimulation differences?
We reviewed and improved our analysis: Fig. 5 (formerly Fig. 4) now does not contain any
significance prior to the onset of stimulation. Bonferroni correction was applied, and this is now
stated in the figure caption.
6. Non-Neuronal Effects: The authors argue that the ECoG responses are “primarily” optogenetically
evoked (non-thermal). However, control experiments indicate substantial non-neuronal effects. Can the
authors estimate the contributions of these two effects (neuronal vs. non-neuronal) to the observed in
vivo data?
Firstly, we have revised our text for improved nuance and clarity in the “Stimulation at rest”
section and throughout the paper.
Secondly, we provide controls which demonstrate that these ECoG data, including the
optogenetically-evoked responses, are neuronal, and we have improved our paper to support
these claims:
1. We provided data with stimulation in expressing and non-expressing areas (Fig. 6)
suggesting significant optogenetic effects.
2. The blue light stimulation results (Fig. 6c) are better explained by optogenetics than thermal
effects (see Discussion paragraph 11 and “Stimulation at rest” paragraph 4).
3. Additional data now added to Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) shows similar stimulation results
between a monkey with no expression (the monkey was never injected with optogenetic
vector) and a monkey with expression that had mostly faded 2 years following viral vector
infusion – both had non-significant increases in stimulation-evoked activity with respect to
baseline, which supports our claims throughout the paper of recording statistically significant
optogenetically-evoked activity from opsin expressing areas.
4. Other controls (e.g., Fig. 5, Fig. 6) further support our finding of an increase in ECoG signals
in response to stimulation of opsin expressing areas.
Thirdly, we have a few comments regarding disentangling “neuronal vs. non-neuronal” effects:
1. The light-evoked artifact in the ECoG signals is non-neuronal and is rejected with a rigorous
process that estimates and then rejects non-neuronal signals with a rigorous PCA-based
algorithm which estimates light-evoked in vivo ECoG artifacts with ECoG recordings of light-
evoked artifacts generated in a neuron-free environment (see the “Photo-induced artifact
removal” sections in both the Results and Methods).
2. We have updated the text to explain that we expected neural network effects to propagate
optogenetically-evoked neural activity after the end of stimulation (see “Stimulation at rest”
paragraph 4), and into opsin deficient regions (see Discussion paragraph 8), which makes
some neuronal responses difficult to predict.
3. Regarding the distinction between thermal and optogenetically evoked responses, we have
conducted extensive experiments and included multiple controls—such as stimulation with
different wavelengths, a naïve animal with no viral injection, brain areas lacking opsin
expression, and time points after expression had decayed. Across all these conditions, our
findings consistently support that the observed responses are optogenetically evoked. If any
thermal effects are present, they are minimal and not significant.
Due to these data and discussion points, we conclude that we have removed a substantial
amount of non-neuronal light-evoked artifact and while the net result may contain some small
degree of thermally-evoked neuronal responses, our controls and simulation work indicate that
we have recorded a substantial amount of optogenetically-evoked neuronal data. Elsewhere in
this response and in the updated paper (e.g., Discussion paragraphs 8 and 9) we reason why the
ECoG recordings were unexpectedly increased due to the activation of Jaws, rather than
decreased.
7. Behavioral Data Statistical Analysis: Was a correction for multiple comparisons applied to the
behavioral data? If not, I suggest this be done to ensure the robustness of the results.
Our initial experimental design focused on examining how stimulation would affect behavioral
metrics, including reach time, path length and reach direction, which we carefully recorded. For
these hypotheses, we did not adjust p-values as the nature of our hypotheses were not
exploratory.
We have updated the manuscript to clarify this distinction. Additionally, in response to the
Reviewers' comments, we have substantially reorganized the behavioral data and corresponding
text to better highlight the technological contributions of our platform.
8. Spatially-Specific Behavioral Effects: I was surprised by the lack of consistent spatially-specific
behavioral effects. How reliable were these effects across sessions or across trial blocks within the same
session? Test-retest reliability should be shown to strengthen the findings.
We have added new data on optogenetically-evoked behavioral responses across days in Supp.
Fig. 6, which illustrates variability across days and within a session. Please also see the revised
Discussion, paragraph 13, where we explain how our findings are comparable to previous non-
human primate reaching studies involving neural stimulation in motor areas.
Regarding the observation of spatially specific behavioral effects—such as certain reach
directions being impaired while others are unaffected—we agree that this is an intriguing finding
that warrants further investigation. We speculate that differences in opsin expression patterns
across the two animals may underlie the variability in these effects.
9. Figure 6 Significance Indicators: The asterisks indicating significance in Figure 6 do not always match
the descriptions in the text. Please check for accuracy. Were all trials included in the analysis for this
figure?
We have updated the figure and caption to include detailed information about the plots to match
the text. The counts of successful trials (and thus the number of trials used to generate the bar
plots) are reported in Supp. Table 1.
Please note that Fig. 6. has been renumbered to Fig. 7.
10. Figure 7: As mentioned earlier, it would be highly informative to show time-frequency plots for four
different electrode sites (transduced vs. non-transduced and task-modulated vs. non-task-modulated
sites).
To address your comment, newly added data (Fig. 8) more deeply explores activity of example
electrodes in opsin deficient and opsin expressing areas in the context of reach. As shown in Fig.
8b, the majority of electrodes cover areas significantly modulated by reaching behavior.
Based on the feedback from Reviewers, we have substantially reorganized the presentation of
our data, and in doing so have removed the figure the Reviewer references (“Figure 7”) and
instead include a new, and more detailed, Fig. 8.
11. Interpretation of Reaching Behavior: The authors interpret the stimulation-induced changes in
reaching behavior as changes in motor dynamics. However, this region of the parietal cortex is involved
in a variety of interrelated functions, including but not restricted to e.g. attention, multisensory
integration, and decision-making. How do the authors disentangle these contributions from the motor
changes observed in the reaching task?
The text (Discussion paragraph 12) has been updated to address this concern. Our study is meant
to be a proof-of-concept that cortical areas modulated with an inhibitory opsin can, indeed,
effect behavior and thus could be a powerful outcome for the sorts of disentanglement
experiments the Reviewer, and others, may devise. Disentangling such functions is an interesting
question that is unfortunately out of scope for this paper as it would require other behavioral
tasks to be performed in conjunction with optogenetic stimulation. Newly added data (Fig. 8,
included in the manuscript due to inspiration from the Reviewer) is another proof of concept of
how our interface can be used to intervene with the brain function and study network dynamic in
correlation with behavioral modulation.

Response to reviewer 3:
I acknowledge the authors’ efforts in addressing my previous concerns and enhancing
the manuscript’s clarity.
We thank reviewer 3 for their continued consideration of this manuscript.
Nonetheless, I remain unconvinced by the explanation provided for the observed
increase in ECoG power during rest. The authors attribute this rise to “disinhibition of
neurons in lower cortical layers following inhibition of upper cortical layers,” yet no direct
recordings from distinct cortical layers were conducted to substantiate this claim.
Moreover, given that the results were obtained after removing stimulation artifacts
through a modeled approach, the possibility that this increase represents an artifact
cannot be dismissed. This issue is pivotal for the robust validation of the platform.
Therefore, I strongly recommend that the authors pursue a more rigorous experimental
approach rather than relying solely on simulations to confirm this phenomenon. For
instance, injecting the same virus into a naive monkey and examining neural responses
across cortical layers during light stimulation would provide more definitive evidence.
We appreciate the Reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion regarding the additional
experiment. At this stage, however, it is not feasible for us to perform this
experiment in our current animals because our platform is not designed for depth
recordings, and conducting the work in a new naïve animal would raise ethical
concerns relative to the 3Rs principles.
That said, we took the previous round of Reviewer feedback very seriously. In
response to the detailed comments and questions, we carried out extensive
additional data collection and analysis using both previously studied animals and
a naïve animal, and we substantially revised and reorganized the manuscript and
figures. We believe these new additions further confirm that the neural responses
we observe are optogenetically induced. In addition, in this recent version of the
manuscript, we have included data from the second monkey (H) after reinjection
(fig. 6f) which further strengthens our results. As a reminder, below we are listing
all additional data and changes to the manuscript in response to the reviewer’s
first round of comments.
Highlights of new data added to the manuscript include:
• Control data from a naïve monkey.
• Control data from one of our animals approximately two years after injection.
• Evidence of renewed optogenetic-evoked activity following reinjection of the
optogenetic viral vector.
• Data and analyses showing how opsin-expressing and opsin-deficient areas
influence neural activity with and without behavior.
• Additional longitudinal neural and behavioral data.
• Measurements of optically induced temperature changes.
• Expanded details on our artifact-rejection method.
Highlights of new analyses and discussion include:
• A new simulation component that supports our in vivo ECoG findings.
• Refined behavioral analyses and strengthened comparisons with related
literature.
• A clearer mechanistic explanation for why inhibitory opsin stimulation could
increase ECoG activity, supported by new in vivo and simulation data, additional
analyses, and an expanded literature review.
Additionally, I suggest the authors broaden their investigation to elucidate the differential
effects observed between LED and laser stimulation. Specifically, it is important to
clarify why laser stimulation, as shown in Figure 5, produces a more focal yet prolonged
activation compared to LED. Addressing these points will significantly strengthen the
manuscript’s scientific rigor and impact.
From a hardware perspective, we believe that the focal, collimated nature of
laser stimulation will naturally produce different effects than the less focal,
uncollimated nature of LED stimulation. With that, we believe it is possible for the
highly focal effects of laser stimulation to evoke local neural responses that
persist, to some degree, after the termination of stimulation. We have updated
the results and discussion sections accordingly.
From the perspective of neuronal circuitry, we believe the prolonged neural
response is probably the result of neural network complexities, including the
possibility of rebound effect (Shapiro et al., 2025, J Physiology). The observation
of rebound effect in simulation also corroborates in vivo stimulation data. This is
now added to the results section.
We also realized that the differences in the colorbar scales between the laser
and LED stimulation conditions could be confusing and might lead to incorrect
visual comparisons. To avoid this and improve clarity, we adjusted the scales so
they are now consistent across both conditions.

The authors addressed all my comments.
