Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Griggs and colleagues present an integrated optogenetic and electrocorticography (ECoG) platform
designed for use in macaques. This is an impressive technical achievement, combining optogenetic
modulation with large-scale neural recordings. While similar techniques have been proposed individually
or with more complex approaches, this tool seems relatively straightforward to implement in a lab with
enough technical expertise. I highly commend the authors for developing and utilizing such an innovative
piece of technology. I’m convinced many will be interested in these tools.
However, I find myself less convinced by the neuroscientific aspects of the manuscript. As the authors
themselves highlight, it is puzzling to observe a net increase in LFP power following Jaws stimulation.
While optogenetic stimulation with a hyperpolarizing opsin is known to induce a mixture of inhibitory
and excitatory effects at the single-unit level, population-level effects should generally lead to net
inhibition.
We thank the Reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback and have addressed their
concern through several key additions and analyses:
1. We introduced a new simulation arm to further investigate the unexpected increase in ECoG
power. The results of this simulation are consistent with our in vivo findings and are presented in
the final paragraph of the “Stimulation at rest” section, Supp. Fig. 5, and the updated Discussion
(paragraphs 9 and 10).
2. We added new data to Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) comparing stimulation responses in a naïve
monkey (with no optogenetic vector injection) and another monkey in which opsin expression
had largely faded two years post-infusion. In both cases, stimulation-evoked activity did not
significantly increase relative to baseline, supporting our claim that the statistically significant
evoked responses reported throughout the paper originate from opsin-expressing cortical
regions
3. We revised the Discussion (paragraphs 8 and 9) to provide a more detailed explanation of the
observed ECoG signal increases, supported by relevant literature. We also reference our previous
work [11], [12], in which we simultaneously recorded from multiple cortical depths while
stimulating and recording from the surface using ECoG electrodes. Those findings are consistent
with the present results and further validate the reported increase in ECoG activity.
These changes, along with our controls (e.g., Fig. 5, Fig. 6), support our finding of an increase in
ECoG signals.
The weak behavioral effects observed also suggest that the output of the stimulated region might be
slightly reduced, which contradicts the observed increase in LFP power. In my view, this unexpected
result warrants further explanation and exploration. Given the substantial light-induced artifacts
observed in saline (Fig. S5), I am still uncertain whether these effects are truly neuronal, despite the
authors’ counter-arguments.
Thank you for your interesting and thoughtful interpretations. We address these concerns in
multiple ways:
1. In our observed data, optogenetic stimulation of the posterior parietal cortex (PPC)—a
region indirectly involved in reaching—produced behavioral effects comparable to those
reported in other non-human primate (NHP) studies using electrical stimulation of motor or
premotor areas that are directly involved in reach control. As noted in the literature,
optogenetically evoked behavioral effects have been difficult to achieve. The fact that we
observed such effects from PPC stimulation, despite it not being a primary motor area,
highlights the strength of our interface: it is capable of optically modulating circuits on a
sufficiently large scale to induce measurable behavioral outcomes. We have clarified this
distinction in the Discussion, paragraphs 12 and 13.
2. Our behavioral measures demonstrate impaired reaching performance following optogenetic
stimulation. As discussed above, the observed delays are comparable to those reported with
excitatory stimulation (e.g., electrical stimulation), suggesting that in both cases, circuit
disruption is the likely underlying mechanism. Understanding the precise downstream neural
effects would require additional experiments, which are beyond the scope of the current
study.
3. We recognized that photo-induced artifacts are apparent in the ECoG signals, and therefore
we developed an effective method of removing photo-induced artifacts. We now include a
brief description of the method in the Results section (“Photo-induced artifact removal”) as
well as a more detailed description in the Methods section (“Photo-induced artifact
removal”).
4. In response to the general concern regarding our unexpected finding that activation of an
inhibitory opsin led to increased ECoG power, we have made substantial revisions to the
manuscript. These additions—including new data and improved contextual explanations—
collectively strengthen the validity of our findings:
a. We introduced a new simulation model to further investigate the observed increase in
ECoG power. The simulation results are consistent with our in vivo data (see the final
paragraph of the “Stimulation at rest” section, Supp. Fig. 5, and Discussion paragraphs 9
and 10).
b. We added data examining the relationship between opsin expression and neural
activity during reach behavior (see the final paragraph of the Results section and Fig. 8).
c. We expanded Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) to include longitudinal stimulation data.
d. We also included stimulation results from a naïve (non-expressing) animal (Fig. 6d).
This animal, along with another in which opsin expression had faded over time, showed
no significant stimulation-evoked activity relative to baseline. These data further support
our claim that significant responses were specific to opsin-expressing regions.
e. We expanded our discussion of the functional roles of areas 5 and 7 in reaching
behavior, incorporating relevant literature as suggested (see Discussion, paragraph 12).
Together with our control data (e.g., Figs. 5 and 6), these revisions provide a more
comprehensive and well-supported interpretation of the observed increase in ECoG activity.
Please note that Supp. Fig. 5 has been split into two new places: Fig. 4 and Supp. Fig. 8.
I was surprised that the authors averaged their results across all ECoG channels (Fig. 4 G-O; 7). Surely, in
Figure 5, they distinguish between transduced and non-transduced sectors. I recommend that they apply
a similar analysis based on the functional properties of the cortex under the electrodes. For example, by
using task-induced neuronal activity (such as reaching-related activity) from both transduced and non-
transduced areas, they could define regions of interest (ROIs) across 4 different cortical regions
(transduced or not, functionally relevant or not). This would allow for a more refined analysis of the
data.
In response, we have revised the manuscript to include data from individual electrodes,
separated by opsin expression status, behavioral and stimulation state and removed the previous
Fig. 7, which pooled data across conditions. We believe that the revised Figs. 5 and 6, and newly
added Fig. 8, now address the Reviewer’s concerns more effectively.
Specifically, Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) now distinguishes between electrodes located in opsin-
expressing versus non-expressing regions. In addition, we have collected and incorporated new
data comparing reach-related activity between stimulated and non-stimulated conditions, and
between opsin-expressing and non-expressing areas, as suggested by the Reviewer (Fig. 8).
As shown in Fig. 8b, ECoG signals from the majority of electrodes are modulated by reach
behavior. This is consistent with the role of the PPC, which is known to support complex
multisensory integration for goal-directed actions. Unlike the motor and somatosensory
cortices—which are more precisely subdivided by body part—the PPC integrates information
across modalities and effectors, and such broad activation is expected.
Please note that Figs. 4 and 5 have been renumbered as Figs. 5 and 6, respectively.
Moreover, it would be valuable to replicate these experiments using a penetrating electrode (e.g., a
laminar probe) to compare the surprising ECoG data with single- or multi-unit recordings, providing
additional insight into the neuronal effects.
While we agree that this is an exciting direction, it is unfortunately beyond the scope of the
current study, as our present platform design does not support simultaneous ECoG and depth
recordings during optical stimulation.
However, to further investigate the unexpected increase in ECoG power, we have added a new
optogenetic simulation model to the study. This model allows for simulated recordings of both
spikes and LFPs at multiple cortical depths during surface optical stimulation. The simulation
results are consistent with our in vivo findings (see the final paragraph of the “Stimulation at
rest” section, Supplementary Fig. 5, and Discussion paragraphs 9 and 10).
In addition, we compare our results to previous work in which we recorded simultaneously from
various cortical depths and the brain surface using ECoG during surface stimulation [11], [12].
Those findings also align well with the observations reported in this study.
In summary, this is a highly interesting technical paper that somehow should be published, but I believe
it should be considered for its methodological contributions rather than its neuroscientific conclusions.
As such, I am presently unconvinced it is suitable for publication in Nature Communications. IMHO, a
more thorough investigation of the neuronal and behavioral effects (see below) is warranted, but I
refrain to the editors to make that call.
Minor Comments:
1. Method Limitations: The authors highlight the advantages of their new method but should also
mention its limitations. For example, the method is limited to recording from superficial, easily
accessible parts of the cortex and cannot capture data from structures buried in sulci or from deeper
cortical areas that are not accessible with the current setup. Surely, more limitations can be listed.
While we do not include a formal limitations section, we have acknowledged the limitations of
our system throughout the Discussion. These include finite temporal and spatial optical access,
a restriction to 32 recording channels, the invasiveness of the chamber implantation procedure,
and other practical considerations.
2. Neuronal Data with Dura Resection: The authors mention that their MMAD allows recording for 10-14
weeks, after which dura growth requires resection. While stability of GFP expression is clearly illustrated
in Figure 3, it would be informative to include raw neuronal traces for the same periods, along with both
GFP and neuronal data after multiple dura resections (e.g., approximately 2-3 years post-implant).
In response, we have:
1. Added ECoG traces in Fig. 4.
2. Added epifluorescence data after 97 weeks in Monkey H (Fig. 6b) and before and after
reinjection in Monkey L (Fig. 6e, insets).
3. Added ECoG data of electrodes in opsin expressing and deficient regions across time (Fig. 6e).
The data include stimulation-evoked ECoG responses after initial injection, reinjection, and
dura resection. Please note that most of the sessions report statistically significant responses.
3. Figure 3C: This figure requires more explanation. It is unclear what point the authors are trying to
make, and further clarification would be helpful.
The figure has been reconfigured as a pie-graph for clarity.
4. Figure 4: The fonts and arrowheads in this figure are barely visible. Please increase their size for better
clarity.
We have enlarged Fig. 5 (formerly Fig. 4) and improved its resolution.
5. Figure 4 Statistical Analysis: I suspect the statistics in Figure 4 use a Wilcoxon signed-rank test. It is
unusual to observe significant changes in the pre-stimulation period. Was a correction for multiple
comparisons applied? If not, this should be done. If a correction was applied, could the authors explain
the pre-stimulation differences?
We reviewed and improved our analysis: Fig. 5 (formerly Fig. 4) now does not contain any
significance prior to the onset of stimulation. Bonferroni correction was applied, and this is now
stated in the figure caption.
6. Non-Neuronal Effects: The authors argue that the ECoG responses are “primarily” optogenetically
evoked (non-thermal). However, control experiments indicate substantial non-neuronal effects. Can the
authors estimate the contributions of these two effects (neuronal vs. non-neuronal) to the observed in
vivo data?
Firstly, we have revised our text for improved nuance and clarity in the “Stimulation at rest”
section and throughout the paper.
Secondly, we provide controls which demonstrate that these ECoG data, including the
optogenetically-evoked responses, are neuronal, and we have improved our paper to support
these claims:
1. We provided data with stimulation in expressing and non-expressing areas (Fig. 6)
suggesting significant optogenetic effects.
2. The blue light stimulation results (Fig. 6c) are better explained by optogenetics than thermal
effects (see Discussion paragraph 11 and “Stimulation at rest” paragraph 4).
3. Additional data now added to Fig. 6 (formerly Fig. 5) shows similar stimulation results
between a monkey with no expression (the monkey was never injected with optogenetic
vector) and a monkey with expression that had mostly faded 2 years following viral vector
infusion – both had non-significant increases in stimulation-evoked activity with respect to
baseline, which supports our claims throughout the paper of recording statistically significant
optogenetically-evoked activity from opsin expressing areas.
4. Other controls (e.g., Fig. 5, Fig. 6) further support our finding of an increase in ECoG signals
in response to stimulation of opsin expressing areas.
Thirdly, we have a few comments regarding disentangling “neuronal vs. non-neuronal” effects:
1. The light-evoked artifact in the ECoG signals is non-neuronal and is rejected with a rigorous
process that estimates and then rejects non-neuronal signals with a rigorous PCA-based
algorithm which estimates light-evoked in vivo ECoG artifacts with ECoG recordings of light-
evoked artifacts generated in a neuron-free environment (see the “Photo-induced artifact
removal” sections in both the Results and Methods).
2. We have updated the text to explain that we expected neural network effects to propagate
optogenetically-evoked neural activity after the end of stimulation (see “Stimulation at rest”
paragraph 4), and into opsin deficient regions (see Discussion paragraph 8), which makes
some neuronal responses difficult to predict.
3. Regarding the distinction between thermal and optogenetically evoked responses, we have
conducted extensive experiments and included multiple controls—such as stimulation with
different wavelengths, a naïve animal with no viral injection, brain areas lacking opsin
expression, and time points after expression had decayed. Across all these conditions, our
findings consistently support that the observed responses are optogenetically evoked. If any
thermal effects are present, they are minimal and not significant.
Due to these data and discussion points, we conclude that we have removed a substantial
amount of non-neuronal light-evoked artifact and while the net result may contain some small
degree of thermally-evoked neuronal responses, our controls and simulation work indicate that
we have recorded a substantial amount of optogenetically-evoked neuronal data. Elsewhere in
this response and in the updated paper (e.g., Discussion paragraphs 8 and 9) we reason why the
ECoG recordings were unexpectedly increased due to the activation of Jaws, rather than
decreased.
7. Behavioral Data Statistical Analysis: Was a correction for multiple comparisons applied to the
behavioral data? If not, I suggest this be done to ensure the robustness of the results.
Our initial experimental design focused on examining how stimulation would affect behavioral
metrics, including reach time, path length and reach direction, which we carefully recorded. For
these hypotheses, we did not adjust p-values as the nature of our hypotheses were not
exploratory.
We have updated the manuscript to clarify this distinction. Additionally, in response to the
Reviewers' comments, we have substantially reorganized the behavioral data and corresponding
text to better highlight the technological contributions of our platform.
8. Spatially-Specific Behavioral Effects: I was surprised by the lack of consistent spatially-specific
behavioral effects. How reliable were these effects across sessions or across trial blocks within the same
session? Test-retest reliability should be shown to strengthen the findings.
We have added new data on optogenetically-evoked behavioral responses across days in Supp.
Fig. 6, which illustrates variability across days and within a session. Please also see the revised
Discussion, paragraph 13, where we explain how our findings are comparable to previous non-
human primate reaching studies involving neural stimulation in motor areas.
Regarding the observation of spatially specific behavioral effects—such as certain reach
directions being impaired while others are unaffected—we agree that this is an intriguing finding
that warrants further investigation. We speculate that differences in opsin expression patterns
across the two animals may underlie the variability in these effects.
9. Figure 6 Significance Indicators: The asterisks indicating significance in Figure 6 do not always match
the descriptions in the text. Please check for accuracy. Were all trials included in the analysis for this
figure?
We have updated the figure and caption to include detailed information about the plots to match
the text. The counts of successful trials (and thus the number of trials used to generate the bar
plots) are reported in Supp. Table 1.
Please note that Fig. 6. has been renumbered to Fig. 7.
10. Figure 7: As mentioned earlier, it would be highly informative to show time-frequency plots for four
different electrode sites (transduced vs. non-transduced and task-modulated vs. non-task-modulated
sites).
To address your comment, newly added data (Fig. 8) more deeply explores activity of example
electrodes in opsin deficient and opsin expressing areas in the context of reach. As shown in Fig.
8b, the majority of electrodes cover areas significantly modulated by reaching behavior.
Based on the feedback from Reviewers, we have substantially reorganized the presentation of
our data, and in doing so have removed the figure the Reviewer references (“Figure 7”) and
instead include a new, and more detailed, Fig. 8.
11. Interpretation of Reaching Behavior: The authors interpret the stimulation-induced changes in
reaching behavior as changes in motor dynamics. However, this region of the parietal cortex is involved
in a variety of interrelated functions, including but not restricted to e.g. attention, multisensory
integration, and decision-making. How do the authors disentangle these contributions from the motor
changes observed in the reaching task?
The text (Discussion paragraph 12) has been updated to address this concern. Our study is meant
to be a proof-of-concept that cortical areas modulated with an inhibitory opsin can, indeed,
effect behavior and thus could be a powerful outcome for the sorts of disentanglement
experiments the Reviewer, and others, may devise. Disentangling such functions is an interesting
question that is unfortunately out of scope for this paper as it would require other behavioral
tasks to be performed in conjunction with optogenetic stimulation. Newly added data (Fig. 8,
included in the manuscript due to inspiration from the Reviewer) is another proof of concept of
how our interface can be used to intervene with the brain function and study network dynamic in
correlation with behavioral modulation.

Response to reviewer 1:

Response to reviewer 3:
I acknowledge the authors’ efforts in addressing my previous concerns and enhancing
the manuscript’s clarity.
We thank reviewer 3 for their continued consideration of this manuscript.
Nonetheless, I remain unconvinced by the explanation provided for the observed
increase in ECoG power during rest. The authors attribute this rise to “disinhibition of
neurons in lower cortical layers following inhibition of upper cortical layers,” yet no direct
recordings from distinct cortical layers were conducted to substantiate this claim.
Moreover, given that the results were obtained after removing stimulation artifacts
through a modeled approach, the possibility that this increase represents an artifact
cannot be dismissed. This issue is pivotal for the robust validation of the platform.
Therefore, I strongly recommend that the authors pursue a more rigorous experimental
approach rather than relying solely on simulations to confirm this phenomenon. For
instance, injecting the same virus into a naive monkey and examining neural responses
across cortical layers during light stimulation would provide more definitive evidence.
We appreciate the Reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion regarding the additional
experiment. At this stage, however, it is not feasible for us to perform this
experiment in our current animals because our platform is not designed for depth
recordings, and conducting the work in a new naïve animal would raise ethical
concerns relative to the 3Rs principles.
That said, we took the previous round of Reviewer feedback very seriously. In
response to the detailed comments and questions, we carried out extensive
additional data collection and analysis using both previously studied animals and
a naïve animal, and we substantially revised and reorganized the manuscript and
figures. We believe these new additions further confirm that the neural responses
we observe are optogenetically induced. In addition, in this recent version of the
manuscript, we have included data from the second monkey (H) after reinjection
(fig. 6f) which further strengthens our results. As a reminder, below we are listing
all additional data and changes to the manuscript in response to the reviewer’s
first round of comments.
Highlights of new data added to the manuscript include:
• Control data from a naïve monkey.
• Control data from one of our animals approximately two years after injection.
• Evidence of renewed optogenetic-evoked activity following reinjection of the
optogenetic viral vector.
• Data and analyses showing how opsin-expressing and opsin-deficient areas
influence neural activity with and without behavior.
• Additional longitudinal neural and behavioral data.
• Measurements of optically induced temperature changes.
• Expanded details on our artifact-rejection method.
Highlights of new analyses and discussion include:
• A new simulation component that supports our in vivo ECoG findings.
• Refined behavioral analyses and strengthened comparisons with related
literature.
• A clearer mechanistic explanation for why inhibitory opsin stimulation could
increase ECoG activity, supported by new in vivo and simulation data, additional
analyses, and an expanded literature review.
Additionally, I suggest the authors broaden their investigation to elucidate the differential
effects observed between LED and laser stimulation. Specifically, it is important to
clarify why laser stimulation, as shown in Figure 5, produces a more focal yet prolonged
activation compared to LED. Addressing these points will significantly strengthen the
manuscript’s scientific rigor and impact.
From a hardware perspective, we believe that the focal, collimated nature of
laser stimulation will naturally produce different effects than the less focal,
uncollimated nature of LED stimulation. With that, we believe it is possible for the
highly focal effects of laser stimulation to evoke local neural responses that
persist, to some degree, after the termination of stimulation. We have updated
the results and discussion sections accordingly.
From the perspective of neuronal circuitry, we believe the prolonged neural
response is probably the result of neural network complexities, including the
possibility of rebound effect (Shapiro et al., 2025, J Physiology). The observation
of rebound effect in simulation also corroborates in vivo stimulation data. This is
now added to the results section.
We also realized that the differences in the colorbar scales between the laser
and LED stimulation conditions could be confusing and might lead to incorrect
visual comparisons. To avoid this and improve clarity, we adjusted the scales so
they are now consistent across both conditions.
